articles.title: A member of one body

statement.t: I am a member of one body of reasoning beings, made for a shared life with them.

parts.words: made for a shared life with them

statement.kind: Many pictures, one claim; then its consequences
statement.form: The statement gathers claims 1 and 2. Claim 1 is fused from five passages that use four different pictures: body, city, sunlight, soul; claim 2 from three that say what we are made for. Claims 3 and 4 are what Marcus draws from it; the “because” of claim 5 is the editor’s.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, the two central claims gain a second author, the body picture gains an arch beside it, and the article gains a concrete act, a second exercise and a caution about crowds: I may step back from them, but I must not hate them. He disputes none of Marcus’s claims here.
seneca.statement: The statement stands. With Seneca it gains the arch: we do not only belong together, we hold one another up.

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: we are limbs of a great body
piece.follows: We are all limbs of a great body.
piece.context: Seneca’s short rule for how to treat other people, given after the rule for worshipping the gods. “We” is gods and humans together: all that you see is one.
gives: as limbs share one body

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: Nature brought us forth as kin, since she begot us from the same things and for the same things. She planted in us love for one another and made us fit for fellowship.
piece.follows: Nature made us kin, from the same things and for the same things, and gave us love for one another.
piece.context: Seneca’s short rule for how to treat other people, given after the rule for worshipping the gods. “Us” is all human beings; “she” is Nature.
gives: We are made
for one another

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: no one can live happily who looks only at himself, who turns everything to his own advantage: you must live for another, if you want to live for yourself
piece.follows: No one lives happily for himself alone; to live for myself I have to live for another.
piece.context: Opens on friendship (a friend’s interest is mine), then widens to all fellow men in 48.3. “Another” is any other person, the friend first.
gives: that shared life is our own good

items.label: why
items.t: We hold one another up as the stones of an arch do: without that support the arch falls.
items.why: Marcus has body, city, sunlight and soul. The arch adds something none of them states: that the whole stands only because its parts hold one another up.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Our fellowship is very like an arch of stones, which would fall if the stones did not block one another, and is held up by that very thing
support.follows: Human fellowship stands the way an arch of stones does: only because its parts hold one another up.
support.context: Seneca’s short rule for how to treat other people, given after the rule for worshipping the gods. “Our fellowship” is human fellowship as a whole, not one friendship.

items.label: action
items.t: My hands should be ready for anyone who needs help.
items.why: Marcus’s claim says to aim at the common good. Seneca names what that looks like when someone is in front of me.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: by her command let our hands be ready for those who need help
support.follows: By Nature’s command we should be ready to help those who need help.
support.context: The practical close of Seneca’s short rule for how to treat other people. “Her” is Nature; those to be helped are people in need, like the shipwrecked and the starving just named.

items.label: practice
items.t: I shall keep one line in my heart and on my lips: I am human, and nothing human is foreign to me.
items.why: A second exercise beside Marcus’s own. The line is from the playwright Terence; Seneca quotes it as something to repeat.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Let that verse be both in the heart and on the lips: “I am human: I count nothing human foreign to me.”
support.follows: I should keep ready a line that says nothing human is foreign to me.
support.context: Seneca’s short rule for how to treat other people, given after the rule for worshipping the gods. “That verse” is a line of Terence, unnamed here, that Lucilius is told to keep ready.

items.label: breaks
items.t: I should not become an enemy to the many for being unlike me. I may withdraw into myself as far as I can, and keep the company that makes me better and that I can make better.
items.why: Marcus says that hating cuts me off. Seneca, writing about crowds that unsettle a character not yet firm, forbids the hatred and still advises stepping back. He does not speak of cutting off, so this is an addition, not a dispute.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: do not become an enemy to many because they are unlike you. Withdraw into yourself as far as you can; keep company with those who will make you better, and let in those whom you in your turn can make better.
support.follows: I should not become an enemy to the crowd for being unlike me; I should withdraw into myself as far as I can and keep company that makes me better and that I can make better.
support.context: A letter on avoiding crowds, which unsettle a character not yet firm. “Many” is the crowd, as at the games; “withdraw” is from it, not from everyone.

passages.title: On why advice needs underlying principles
passages.text: All this that you see, in which things divine and human are enclosed, is one; we are limbs of a great body. Nature brought us forth as kin, since she begot us from the same things and for the same things. She planted in us love for one another and made us fit for fellowship. She established what is fair and just; by her arrangement it is more wretched to harm than to be hurt; by her command let our hands be ready for those who need help.

passages.title: On logic puzzles versus real help
passages.text: Am I talking like an Epicurean again? But in fact the same thing is in my interest as is in yours: or else I am no friend, if whatever matter concerns you is not mine. Friendship makes between us a partnership in all things. Nothing favourable and nothing adverse belongs to one alone; life is lived in common. And no one can live happily who looks only at himself, who turns everything to his own advantage: you must live for another, if you want to live for yourself.

passages.title: On why advice needs underlying principles
passages.text: Let that verse be both in the heart and on the lips: “I am human: I count nothing human foreign to me.” Let us have it in common: we have been born. Our fellowship is very like an arch of stones, which would fall if the stones did not block one another, and is held up by that very thing.

passages.title: On avoiding the crowd
passages.text: You are bound either to imitate or to hate. But both are to be avoided: do not become like the bad because they are many, and do not become an enemy to many because they are unlike you. Withdraw into yourself as far as you can; keep company with those who will make you better, and let in those whom you in your turn can make better. This works both ways, and people learn while they teach.

claims.t: Everything that reasons shares one reason, as limbs share one body, citizens one city, and every lit place one sun.
claims.shared: Four pictures (body, city, sunlight, soul) with one structure: a single thing present in many, and not split by being shared.
claims.changed: Marcus says “one soul that has mind” in 12.23 and 9.7, and “mind” and “reason” in 4.4. The fused claim says “reason” throughout.

support.quote: The relation that the limbs of the body have in things that are united is the relation that rational beings have in things that stand apart
support.follows: Rational beings, who stand apart, have the same relation to one another that the limbs of one body have.
gives: as limbs share one body
Everything that reasons

support.quote: we are citizens. If that is so, we share in some civic body. If that is so, the universe is, as it were, a city.
support.follows: We are citizens, we share in a civic body, and the universe is like a city.
gives: citizens one city
support.note: The last step of a chain that starts from mind and reason being common to us.

support.quote: you yourself help to complete a civic whole
support.follows: I am one of those who make a civic whole complete.
gives: citizens one city
support.note: Casaubon wrote that I was “made for” a common society. The Greek has no making here: one word says that I am one of the things that make the civic whole complete.

support.quote: One light of the sun, even if it is divided by walls, by mountains
support.follows: The light of the sun is one, even where walls and mountains divide it.
gives: every lit place one sun

support.quote: One soul that has mind, even if it seems to be separated.
support.follows: There is one soul that has mind, even though it seems to be separated.
gives: shares one reason

support.quote: one soul that has mind has been portioned out among the rational ones
support.follows: The beings that reason share one soul, the soul that has mind.
gives: shares one reason
Everything that reasons

claims.t: We are made for one another and for one common work, and that shared life is our own good.
claims.shared: Each says that a rational being is directed toward its own kind, whether by what it was built or born for (7.10, 5.15) or by the nature it shares in (9.7). 5.15 and 9.7 both say the direction is toward one another, and 5.15 and 7.10 both call it its own good.

support.quote: being built to do some one work together
support.follows: Rational beings are built to do one work together.
gives: for one common work
We are made

support.quote: everything that shares in a common nature of mind hurries toward its kin in the same way, or even more
support.follows: Whatever shares in the common nature of mind hurries toward its own kin.
gives: for one another

support.quote: therefore the good of a rational animal is community
support.follows: Living with others is what is good for a reasoning being.
gives: that shared life is our own good

support.quote: For that we were born for community has long since been shown.
support.follows: It has long been shown that we were born for community.
gives: We are made

support.quote: the worse things are for the sake of the better, and the better for the sake of one another? And things with a soul are better than things without one, and rational things better than things with a soul.
support.follows: The better things are for the sake of one another, and rational things rank above everything else that has a soul.
gives: for one another
support.note: Asked as a question that expects the answer yes: the better things are for the sake of one another. Marcus then ranks rational things highest.

support.quote: doing good does not yet delight you fully; you still do it as no more than the proper thing, not yet as doing good to yourself
support.follows: Doing good is also doing good to myself, and I have not grasped that while I do it only because it is proper.
gives: our own good
support.note: Marcus’s word for “doing good” means doing a kindness to someone else. The good of the other and my own are the same act.

claims.t: So each thing I do should aim at the common good, directly or at a distance, and holding to that one aim is what makes me one person.
claims.shared: Two passages set the same aim for what I do: 9.21 calls it “the social goal”, 11.19 “the social and civic one”. 11.19 adds what the single aim does for the one who holds it: that person is always the same. 9.21 gives the reverse case: an action without that reference “tears your life apart and does not let it be one”.

support.quote: so too let every action of yours help to complete a civic life
support.follows: Every action of mine should help to complete a civic life.
gives: each thing I do should

support.quote: any action of yours that does not refer, whether directly or at a distance, to the social goal tears your life apart and does not let it be one
support.follows: An action with no reference to the social goal, not even a distant one, tears my life apart and keeps it from being one.
gives: directly or at a distance
aim at the common good

support.quote: so too the aim to be set up must be the social and civic one
support.follows: The aim I set up should be the social and civic one.
gives: aim at the common good
support.note: In the same sentence Marcus compares this aim to “the common goods”, the only goods that people judge alike.

support.quote: whoever directs all their private impulses toward this aim will make all their actions alike, and in this way will always be the same
support.follows: A person who directs every private impulse toward this aim makes all their actions alike, and so is always the same.
gives: holding to that one aim is what makes me one person

claims.t: When I hate someone, wrong them, or resent what happens, I cut myself off, and not from that one thing only but from the whole.
claims.shared: Three pictures of severing (a branch, a limb, a seditious citizen). In each the person does it to himself, and in each the cut is from the whole.

support.quote: it is the human being who separates themselves from their neighbour, by coming to hate and turning away
support.follows: A person separates themselves from a neighbour by coming to hate and turning away.
gives: When I hate someone
I cut myself off

support.quote: they do not know that they have at the same time cut themselves away from the whole civic body as well
support.follows: In the same act, and without knowing it, he separates himself from the whole body of people.
gives: from the whole

support.quote: If you have ever seen a hand cut off, or a foot, or a severed head, lying somewhere or other apart from the rest of the body: that is what a person makes of themselves, as far as it is in their power, when they do not want what happens
support.follows: A person who does not want what happens makes of themselves, as far as they can, something like a hand or foot cut off from the body.
gives: resent what happens
support.note: 8.32 counts not wanting what happens as a cut too.

support.quote: or when they do something unsocial
support.follows: Doing something unsocial is counted as the same kind of act.
gives: wrong them

support.quote: he put it in the human being’s power not to be broken off from the whole in the first place
support.follows: It is in a person’s own power not to be broken off from the whole.
gives: I cut myself off
from the whole

support.quote: like the person in a citizen body who, for their own part, stands apart from such harmony
support.follows: It is like a person in a body of citizens who, for their own part, stands apart from its harmony.
gives: I cut myself off

claims.t: Having cut myself off, I can grow back into the whole, because nature is stronger than my leaving.
claims.shared: Two passages say the return is possible in almost the same words. 9.7 says something else: those who run away are overtaken all the same, because nature prevails. Joining the two with “because” is the editor’s step.
claims.changed: 11.7 credits the return to Zeus and 8.32 to god. The fused claim credits nature, following 9.7.

inferences.why: No passage gives this reason: 11.7 credits the return to Zeus and 8.32 to god, and 9.7 speaks of people who run away and are overtaken, not of a return.

support.quote: we are allowed to grow together again with the one next to us and again to help to complete the whole
support.follows: We are allowed to grow together again with the person next to us, and again to help make the whole complete.
gives: I can grow back into the whole

support.quote: for one who has been broken off, he made it possible to come back again and grow together
support.follows: A person who has been broken off has been given the power to come back and grow together again.
gives: I can grow back

support.quote: though they run away, they are overtaken and hemmed in all the same; for nature prevails
support.follows: Those who run away are overtaken all the same, because nature prevails.
gives: nature is stronger than my leaving

single.quote: you often say to yourself: “I am a limb [melos] of the whole made up of rational beings.”
single.label: A practice
single.t: I shall often say to myself: I am a member, and not merely a part.
single.why: Only 7.10 gives an exercise. It is kept as the article’s practice.
single.follows: I should often tell myself that I am a limb of the whole that rational beings make up.

single.quote: when this kind of division happens many times, it makes what withdraws hard to unite and hard to restore
single.label: A warning
single.t: The more often I cut myself off, the harder the return.
single.why: Only 11.7 says the return gets harder. One witness, so it is not fused into claim 5.
single.follows: When this division happens many times, what withdraws becomes hard to unite and hard to restore.

members.text:
Of all unreasonable creatures, there is but one unreasonable soul;
and of all that are reasonable, but one reasonable soul, divided betwixt
them all. As of all earthly things there is but one earth, and but one
light that we see by; and but one air that we breathe in, as many as
either breathe or see. Now whatsoever partakes of some common thing,
naturally affects and inclines unto that whereof it is part, being of
one kind and nature with it. Whatsoever is earthly, presseth downwards
to the common earth. Whatsoever is liquid, would flow together. And
whatsoever is airy, would be together likewise. So that without some
obstacle, and some kind of violence, they cannot well be kept asunder.
Whatsoever is fiery, doth not only by reason of the elementary fire tend
upwards; but here also is so ready to join, and to burn together, that
whatsoever doth want sufficient moisture to make resistance, is easily
set on fire. Whatsoever therefore is partaker of that reasonable common
nature, naturally doth as much and more long after his own kind. For by
how much in its own nature it excels all other things, by so much more
is it desirous to be joined and united unto that, which is of its own
nature. As for unreasonable creatures then, they had not long been, but
presently begun among them swarms, and flocks, and broods of young ones,
and a kind of mutual love and affection. For though but unreasonable,
yet a kind of soul these had, and therefore was that natural desire of
union more strong and intense in them, as in creatures of a more
excellent nature, than either in plants, or stones, or trees. But among
reasonable creatures, begun commonwealths, friendships, families, public
meetings, and even in their wars, conventions, and truces. Now among
them that were yet of a more excellent nature, as the stars and planets,
though by their nature far distant one from another, yet even among them
began some mutual correspondency and unity. So proper is it to
excellency in a high degree to affect unity, as that even in things so
far distant, it could operate unto a mutual sympathy. But now behold,
what is now come to pass. Those creatures that are reasonable, are now
the only creatures that have forgotten their natural affection and
inclination of one towards another. Among them alone of all other things
that are of one kind, there is not to be found a general disposition to
flow together. But though they fly from nature, yet are they stopt in
their course, and apprehended. Do they what they can, nature doth
prevail. And so shalt thou confess, if thou dost observe it. For sooner
mayst thou find a thing earthly, where no earthly thing is, than find a
man that naturally can live by himself alone.
members.english:
One soul has been divided among the animals without reason, and one soul that has mind has been portioned out among the rational ones, just as there is one earth for all earthy things, and we see by one light and breathe one air, all of us that have sight and a soul.

All things that share in something common hurry toward what is of their own kind. Everything earthy tends toward earth. Everything wet flows together. What is airy does the same, so that it takes things to hold them apart, and force. Fire is carried upward because of the elemental fire, yet it is so ready to be kindled together with every fire here that even everything material that is a little drier is easy to kindle, because less of what hinders kindling is mixed into it. So too, then, everything that shares in a common nature of mind hurries toward its kin in the same way, or even more. For the better it is compared with the rest, the readier it is to mix with what is its own and to be poured together with it. At any rate, right from the start, among the animals without reason there were found swarms and herds and the rearing of nestlings and what one might call loves; for here there were already souls, and the thing that draws together was found growing stronger in what is better, of a kind that did not exist in plants, or in stones or timber. Among the rational animals there were states and friendships and households and gatherings, and in wars treaties and truces. Among those better still, even out of things that stand apart there came to be, in a way, a union, such as there is among the stars. In this way the climb toward the better was able to produce a shared feeling even in things that stand apart. See, then, what is happening now. For only the beings that have mind have now forgotten their hurrying toward one another and their leaning together, and only here is the flowing together not to be seen. And yet, though they run away, they are overtaken and hemmed in all the same; for nature prevails. You will see what I mean if you watch closely. At any rate, one would sooner find something earthy touching nothing earthy than a human being split off from a human being.

members.text:
Such as thy thoughts and ordinary cogitations are, such will thy
mind be in time. For the soul doth as it were receive its tincture from
the fancies, and imaginations. Dye it therefore and thoroughly soak it
with the assiduity of these cogitations. As for example. Wheresoever
thou mayest live, there it is in thy power to live well and happy. But
thou mayest live at the Court, there then also mayest thou live well and
happy. Again, that which everything is made for, he is also made unto
that, and cannot but naturally incline unto it. That which anything
doth naturally incline unto, therein is his end. Wherein the end of
everything doth consist, therein also doth his good and benefit consist.
Society therefore is the proper good of a rational creature. For that we
are made for society, it hath long since been demonstrated. Or can any
man make any question of this, that whatsoever is naturally worse and
inferior, is ordinarily subordinated to that which is better? and that
those things that are best, are made one for another? And those things
that have souls, are better than those that have none? and of those that
have, those best that have rational souls?
members.english: Whatever kind of impressions you often form, your thought will be of that kind; for the soul is dyed by its impressions. So dye it with an unbroken run of impressions such as these. For example: where it is possible to live, there it is also possible to live well; but it is possible to live at court; therefore it is also possible to live well at court. And again: each thing is carried toward that for the sake of which it was built; and what it is carried toward, in that lies its goal; and where its goal is, there also is the benefit and the good of each thing; therefore the good of a rational animal is community. For that we were born for community has long since been shown. Or was it not plain that the worse things are for the sake of the better, and the better for the sake of one another? And things with a soul are better than things without one, and rational things better than things with a soul.
members.greek: Οἷα ἂν πολλάκις φαντασθῇς, τοιαύτη σοι ἔσται ἡ διάνοια· βάπτεται γὰρ ὑπὸ τῶν φαντασιῶν ἡ ψυχή. βάπτε οὐν αὐτὴν τῇ συνεχείᾳ τῶν τοιούτων φαντασιῶν· οἷον, ὅτι ὅπου ζῆν ἐστιν, ἐκεῖ καὶ εὖ ζῆν· ἐν αὐλῇ δὲ ζῆν ἐστιν· ἔστιν ἄρα καὶ εὖ ζῆν ἐν αὐλῇ. καὶ πάλιν, ὅτι οὗπερ ἕνεκεν ἕκαστον κατεσκεύασται, πρὸς τοῦτο φέρεται· πρὸς ὃ φέρεται δέ, ἐν τούτῳ τὸ τέλος αὐτοῦ· ὅπου δὲ τὸ τέλος, ἐκεῖ καὶ τὸ συμφέρον καὶ τὸ ἀγαθὸν ἑκάστου· τὸ ἄρα ἀγαθὸν τοῦ λογικοῦ ζῴου κοινωνία. ὅτι γὰρ πρὸς κοινωνίαν γεγόναμεν, πάλαι δέδεικται· ἢ οὐκ ἦν ἐναργὲς ὅτι τὰ χείρω τῶν κρειττόνων ἕνεκεν, τὰ δὲ κρείττω ἀλλήλων; κρείττω δὲ τῶν μὲν ἀψύχων τὰ ἔμψυχα, τῶν δὲ ἐμψύχων τὰ λογικά.

If ever thou sawest either a hand, or a foot, or a head lying by
itself, in some place or other, as cut off from the rest of the body,
such must thou conceive him to make himself, as much as in him lieth,
that either is offended with anything that is happened, (whatsoever it
be) and as it were divides himself from it: or that commits anything
against the natural law of mutual correspondence, and society among men:
or, he that, commits any act of uncharitableness. Whosoever thou art,
thou art such, thou art cast forth I know not whither out of the general
unity, which is according to nature. Thou went born indeed a part, but
now thou hast cut thyself off. However, herein is matter of joy and
exultation, that thou mayst be united again. God hath not granted
it unto any other part, that once separated and cut off, it might be
reunited, and come together again. But, behold, that GOODNESS how great
and immense it is! which hath so much esteemed MAN. As at first he
was so made, that he needed not, except he would himself, have divided
himself from the whole; so once divided and cut off, IT hath so provided
and ordered it, that if he would himself, he might return, and grow
together again, and be admitted into its former rank and place of a
part, as he was before.
members.english: If you have ever seen a hand cut off, or a foot, or a severed head, lying somewhere or other apart from the rest of the body: that is what a person makes of themselves, as far as it is in their power, when they do not want what happens and split themselves off, or when they do something unsocial. You lie somewhere or other, thrown away from the union that accords with nature; for you were by nature a part, but now you have cut yourself off. But here is the neat thing: you are allowed to unite yourself again. To no other part has god granted this, to come together again once it has been separated and cut through. But consider the kindness with which he has honoured the human being: for he put it in the human being’s power not to be broken off from the whole in the first place, and, for one who has been broken off, he made it possible to come back again and grow together and take up again the place of a part.
members.greek: Εἴ ποτε εἶδες χεῖρα ἀποκεκομμένην ἢ πόδα ἢ κεφαλὴν ἀποτετμημένην, χωρίς πού ποτε ἀπὸ τοῦ λοιποῦ σώματος κειμένην· τοιοῦτον ἑαυτὸν ποιεῖ, ὅσον ἐφ’ ἑαυτῷ, ὁ μὴ θέλων τὸ συμβαῖνον καὶ ἀποσχίζων ἑαυτὸν ἢ ὁ ἀκοινώνητόν τι πράσσων. ἀπέρριψαί πού ποτε ἀπὸ τῆς κατὰ φύσιν ἑνώσεως· ἐπεφύκεις γὰρ μέρος· νῦν δὲ σεαυτὸν ἀπέκοψας. ἀλλ’ ὧδε κομψὸν ἐκεῖνο, ὅτι ἔξεστί σοι πάλιν ἑνῶσαι σεαυτόν. τοῦτο ἄλλῳ μέρει οὐδενὶ θεὸς ἐπέτρεψεν, χωρισθέντι καὶ διακοπέντι πάλιν συνελθεῖν, ἀλλὰ σκέψαι τὴν χρηστότητα ᾗ τετίμηκε τὸν ἄνθρωπον· καὶ γὰρ ἵνα τὴν ἀρχὴν μὴ ἀπορραγῇ ἀπὸ τοῦ ὅλου ἐπ’ αὐτῷ ἐποίησε, καὶ ἀπορραγέντι πάλιν ἐπανελθεῖν καὶ συμφῦναι καὶ τὴν τοῦ μέρους τάξιν ἀπολαβεῖν ἐποίησεν.

members.text:
As several members in one body united, so are reasonable creatures
in a body divided and dispersed, all made and prepared for one common
operation. And this thou shalt apprehend the better, if thou shalt use
thyself often to say to thyself, I am μέλος, or a member of the mass and
body of reasonable substances. But if thou shalt say I am μέρος, or
a part, thou dost not yet love men from thy heart. The joy that thou
takest in the exercise of bounty, is not yet grounded upon a due
ratiocination and right apprehension of the nature of things. Thou dost
exercise it as yet upon this ground barely, as a thing convenient and
fitting; not, as doing good to thyself, when thou dost good unto others.
members.english: The relation that the limbs of the body have in things that are united is the relation that rational beings have in things that stand apart, being built to do some one work together. The thought of this will strike you more if you often say to yourself: “I am a limb [melos] of the whole made up of rational beings.” But if, by using the letter rho, you say that you are a part [meros], you do not yet love people from the heart; doing good does not yet delight you fully; you still do it as no more than the proper thing, not yet as doing good to yourself.
members.greek: Οἷόν ἐστιν ἐν ἡνωμένοις τὰ μέλη τοῦ σώματος, τοῦτον ἔχει τὸν λόγον ἐν διεστῶσι τὰ λογικά, πρὸς μίαν τινὰ συνεργίαν κατεσκευασμένα. μᾶλλον δέ σοι ἡ τούτου νόησις προσπεσεῖται, ἐὰν πρὸς ἑαυτὸν πολλάκις λέγῃς, ὅτι μέλος εἰμὶ τοῦ ἐκ τῶν λογικῶν συστήματος. ἐὰν δὲ διὰ τοῦ ῥῶ στοιχείου μέρος εἶναι ἑαυτὸν λέγῃς, οὔπω ἀπὸ καρδίας φιλεῖς τοὺς ἀνθρώπους· οὔπω σε καταληκτικῶς εὐφραίνει τὸ εὐεργετεῖν· ἔτι ὡς πρέπον αὐτὸ ψιλὸν ποιεῖς, οὔπω ὡς ἑαυτὸν εὖ ποιῶν.

members.text:
If to understand and to be reasonable be common unto all men, then
is that reason, for which we are termed reasonable, common unto all. If
reason is general, then is that reason also, which prescribeth what is
to be done and what not, common unto all. If that, then law. If law,
then are we fellow-citizens. If so, then are we partners in some one
commonweal. If so, then the world is as it were a city. For which other
commonweal is it, that all men can be said to be members of? From this
common city it is, that understanding, reason, and law is derived unto
us, for from whence else? For as that which in me is earthly I have from
some common earth; and that which is moist from some other element is
imparted; as my breath and life hath its proper fountain; and that
likewise which is dry and fiery in me: (for there is nothing which doth
not proceed from something; as also there is nothing that can be reduced
unto mere nothing:) so also is there some common beginning from whence
my understanding hath proceeded.
members.english: If mind is common to us, then reason too, by which we are rational, is common. If that is so, then the reason that commands what is to be done or not done is also common. If that is so, law too is common. If that is so, we are citizens. If that is so, we share in some civic body. If that is so, the universe is, as it were, a city. For in what other common civic body will anyone say that the whole race of human beings shares? And it is from there, from this common city, that our very mind and reason and sense of law come; or from where else? For just as what is earthy in me has been portioned off from some earth, and what is wet from another element, and what is breath from some source, and what is warm and fiery from some source of its own (for nothing comes from nothing, just as nothing goes away into what is not), so too mind has come from somewhere.
members.greek: Εἰ τὸ νοερὸν ἡμῖν κοινόν, καὶ ὁ λόγος, καθʼ ὃν λογικοί ἐσμεν, κοινός· εἰ τοῦτο, καὶ ὁ προστακτικὸς τῶν ποιητέων ἢ μὴ λόγος κοινός· εἰ τοῦτο, καὶ ὁ νόμος κοινός· εἰ τοῦτο, πολῖταί ἐσμεν· εἰ τοῦτο, πολιτεύματός τινος μετέχομεν· εἰ τοῦτο, ὁ κόσμος ὡσανεὶ πόλις ἐστί· τίνος γὰρ ἄλλου φήσει τις τὸ τῶν ἀνθρώπων πᾶν γένος κοινοῦ πολιτεύματος μετέχειν; ἐκεῖθεν δέ, ἐκ τῆς κοινῆς ταύτης πόλεως, καὶ αὐτὸ τὸ νοερὸν καὶ λογικὸν καὶ νομικὸν ἡμῖν ἢ πόθεν; ὥσπερ γὰρ τὸ γεῶδές μοι ἀπό τινος γῆς ἀπομεμέρισται καὶ τὸ ὑγρὸν ἀφʼ ἑτέρου στοιχείου καὶ τὸ πνευματικὸν ἀπὸ πηγῆς τινος καὶ τὸ θερμὸν καὶ πυρῶδες ἔκ τινος ἰδίας πηγῆς (οὐδὲν γὰρ ἐκ τοῦ μηδενὸς ἔρχεται, ὥσπερ μηδʼ εἰς τὸ οὐκ ὂν ἀπέρχεται), οὕτω δὴ καὶ τὸ νοερὸν ἥκει ποθέν.

members.text:
As thou thyself, whoever thou art, were made for the perfection and
consummation, being a member of it, of a common society; so must every
action of thine tend to the perfection and consummation of a life that
is truly sociable. What action soever of thine therefore that either
immediately or afar off, hath not reference to the common good, that is
an exorbitant and disorderly action; yea it is seditious; as one among
the people who from such and such a consent and unity, should factiously
divide and separate himself.
members.english: Just as you yourself help to complete a civic whole, so too let every action of yours help to complete a civic life. So any action of yours that does not refer, whether directly or at a distance, to the social goal tears your life apart and does not let it be one, and it is seditious, like the person in a citizen body who, for their own part, stands apart from such harmony.
members.greek: Ὥσπερ αὐτὸς σὺ πολιτικοῦ συστήματος συμπληρωτικὸς εἶ, οὕτως καὶ πᾶσα πρᾶξίς σου συμπληρωτικὴ ἔστω ζωῆς πολιτικῆς. ἥτις ἐὰν οὖν πρᾶξίς σου μὴ ἔχῃ τὴν ἀναφοράν, εἴτε προσεχῶς εἴτε πόρρωθεν, ἐπὶ τὸ κοινωνικὸν τέλος, αὕτη διασπᾷ τὸν βίον καὶ οὐκ ἐᾷ ἕνα εἶναι καὶ στασιώδης ἐστίν, ὥσπερ ἐν δήμῳ ὁ τὸ καθ’ αὑτὸν μέρος διιστάμενος ἀπὸ τῆς τοιαύτης συμφωνίας.

members.text:
There is but one light of the sun, though it be intercepted by
walls and mountains, and other thousand objects. There is but one common
substance of the whole world, though it be concluded and restrained into
several different bodies, in number infinite. There is but one common
soul, though divided into innumerable particular essences and natures.
So is there but one common intellectual soul, though it seem to be
divided. And as for all other parts of those generals which we have
mentioned, as either sensitive souls or subjects, these of themselves
(as naturally irrational) have no common mutual reference one unto
another, though many of them contain a mind, or reasonable faculty in
them, whereby they are ruled and governed. But of every reasonable mind,
this the particular nature, that it hath reference to whatsoever is
of her own kind, and desireth to be united: neither can this common
affection, or mutual unity and correspondency, be here intercepted or
divided, or confined to particulars as those other common things are.
members.english: One light of the sun, even if it is divided by walls, by mountains, by countless other things. One common substance, even if it is divided by countless bodies, each with its own quality. One soul, even if it is divided by countless natures and individual outlines. One soul that has mind, even if it seems to be separated. Now the other parts of the things just named, such as breaths and the matter that underlies things, are without sensation and have no attachment to one another; and yet even those are held together by what makes them one and by the weight that bears toward the same place. But thought, in a way of its own, stretches toward what is of the same kind and joins with it, and the social feeling is not divided.
members.greek: Ἓν φῶς ἡλίου, κἂν διείργηται τοίχοις, ὄρεσιν, ἄλλοις μυρίοις. μία οὐσία κοινή, κἂν διείργηται ἰδίως ποιοῖς σώμασι μυρίοις. μία ψυχή, κἂν φύσεσι διείργηται μυρίαις καὶ ἰδίαις περιγραφαῖς. μία νοερὰ ψυχή, κἂν διακεκρίσθαι δοκῇ. τὰ μὲν οὖν ἄλλα μέρη τῶν εἰρημένων, οἷον πνεύματα καὶ ὑποκείμενα, ἀναίσθητα καὶ ἀνοικείωτα ἀλλήλοις· καίτοι κἀκεῖνα τὸ ἑνοῦν συνέχει καὶ τὸ ἐπὶ τὰ αὐτὰ βρῖθον. διάνοια δὲ ἰδίως ἐπὶ τὸ ὁμόφυλον τείνεται καὶ συνίσταται καὶ οὐ διείργεται τὸ κοινωνικὸν πάθος.

members.text:
He that hath not one and the self-same general end always as long
as he liveth, cannot possibly be one and the self-same man always. But
this will not suffice except thou add also what ought to be this general
end. For as the general conceit and apprehension of all those things
which upon no certain ground are by the greater part of men deemed good,
cannot be uniform and agreeable, but that only which is limited and
restrained by some certain proprieties and conditions, as of community:
that nothing be conceived good, which is not commonly and publicly
good: so must the end also that we propose unto ourselves, be common
and sociable. For he that doth direct all his own private motions and
purposes to that end, all his actions will be agreeable and uniform; and
by that means will be still the same man.
members.english: “A person who does not always have one and the same aim in life cannot be one and the same through the whole of life.” The saying is not enough unless you also add what kind of aim this must be. For just as judgment is not alike about all the things that in one way or another seem good to the majority, but is alike about those of a certain kind, that is, the common goods, so too the aim to be set up must be the social and civic one. For whoever directs all their private impulses toward this aim will make all their actions alike, and in this way will always be the same.
members.greek: ʽὯι μὴ εἶς καὶ ὁ αὐτός ἐστιν ἀεὶ τοῦ βίου σκοπός, οὗτος εἷς καὶ ὁ αὐτὸς δι’ ὅλου τοῦ βίου εἶναι οὐ δύναται.ʼ οὐκ ἀρκεῖ τὸ εἰρημένον, ἐὰν μὴ κἀκεῖνο προσθῇς, ὁποῖον εἶναι δεῖ τοῦτον τὸν σκοπόν. ὥσπερ γὰρ οὐχ ἡ πάντων τῶν ὁπωσοῦν τοῖς πλείοσι δοκούντων ἀγαθῶν ὑπόληψις ὁμοία ἐστίν, ἀλλ’ ἡ τῶν τοιῶνδέ τινων, τουτέστι τῶν κοινῶν, οὕτω καὶ τὸν σκοπὸν δεῖ τὸν κοινωνικὸν καὶ πολιτικὸν ὑποστήσασθαι. ὁ γὰρ εἰς τοῦτον πάσας τὰς ἰδίας ὁρμὰς ἀπευθύνων πάσας τὰς πράξεις ὁμοίας ἀποδώσει καὶ κατὰ τοῦτο ἀεὶ ὁ αὐτὸς ἔσται.

members.why: A wish to think together with the mind that surrounds all things, as we breathe together with the air around us. Close to claim 1, but a wish and not a statement.
members.text:
Not only now henceforth to have a common breath, or to hold
correspondency of breath, with that air, that compasseth us about; but
to have a common mind, or to hold correspondency of mind also with that
rational substance, which compasseth all things. For, that also is of
itself, and of its own nature (if a man can but draw it in as he should)
everywhere diffused; and passeth through all things, no less than the
air doth, if a man can but suck it in.
members.english: No longer only to breathe together with the surrounding air, but from now on also to think together with the mind that surrounds all things. For the power of mind is poured out everywhere and has spread all through, for the one able to draw it in, no less than the power of air for the one able to breathe it.
members.greek: Μηκέτι μόνον συμπνεῖν τῷ περιέχοντι ἀέρι, ἀλλ’ ἤδη καὶ συμφρονεῖν τῷ περιέχοντι πάντα νοερῷ. οὐ γὰρ ἧττον ἡ νοερὰ δύναμις πάντῃ κέχυται καὶ διαπεφοίτηκε τῷ σπάσαι δυναμένῳ ἤπερ ἡ ἀερώδης τῷ ἀναπνεῦσαι δυναμένῳ.

members.text:
A branch cut off from the continuity of that which was next unto
it, must needs be cut off from the whole tree: so a man that is divided
from another man, is divided from the whole society. A branch is cut off
by another, but he that hates and is averse, cuts himself off from his
neighbour, and knows not that at the same time he divides himself from
the whole body, or corporation. But herein is the gift and mercy of God,
the Author of this society, in that, once cut off we may grow together
and become part of the whole again. But if this happen often the misery
is that the further a man is run in this division, the harder he is to
be reunited and restored again: and however the branch which, once cut
of afterwards was graffed in, gardeners can tell you is not like that
which sprouted together at first, and still continued in the unity of
the body.
members.english: A branch cut off from the branch next to it cannot help being cut off from the whole plant as well. So too a human being split off from one human being has fallen away from the whole community. Now a branch is cut off by someone else; but it is the human being who separates themselves from their neighbour, by coming to hate and turning away, and they do not know that they have at the same time cut themselves away from the whole civic body as well. Yet there is this gift from Zeus, who put the community together: we are allowed to grow together again with the one next to us and again to help to complete the whole. But when this kind of division happens many times, it makes what withdraws hard to unite and hard to restore. And in general, the branch that sprouted together from the beginning and has stayed together, sharing one breath, is not like the one grafted in again after being cut off, whatever it is that the gardeners say.
members.greek: Κλάδος τοῦ προσεχοῦς κλάδου ἀποκοπεὶς οὐ δύναται μὴ καὶ τοῦ ὅλου φυτοῦ ἀποκεκόφθαι. οὕτω δὴ καὶ ἄνθρωπος ἑνὸς ἀνθρώπου ἀποσχισθεὶς ὅλης τῆς κοινωνίας ἀποπέπτωκε. κλάδον μὲν οὖν ἄλλος ἀποκόπτει· ἄνθρωπος δὲ αὐτὸς ἑαυτὸν τοῦ πλησίον χωρίζει μισήσας καὶ ἀποστραφείς, ἀγνοεῖ δὲ ὅτι καὶ τοῦ ὅλου πολιτεύματος ἅμα ἀποτέτμηκεν ἑαυτόν. πλὴν ἐκεῖνό γε δῶρον τοῦ συστησαμένου τὴν κοινωνίαν Διός· ἔξεστι γὰρ ἡμῖν πάλιν συμφῦναι τῷ προσεχεῖ καὶ πάλιν τοῦ ὅλου συμπληρωτικοῖς γενέσθαι. πλεονάκις μέντοι γινόμενον τὸ κατὰ τὴν τοιαύτην διαίρεσιν δυσένωτον καὶ δυσαποκατάστατον τὸ ἀποχωροῦν ποιεῖ. ὅλως τε οὐχ ὅμοιος ὁ κλάδος ὁ ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς συμβλαστήσας καὶ σύμπνους συμμείνας τῷ μετὰ τὴν ἀποκοπὴν αὖθις ἐγκεντρισθέντι, ὅ τι ποτὲ λέγουσιν οἱ φυτουργοί.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek instead of Casaubon. Passage numbers stay Casaubon’s. In modern editions 9.7 is 9.8 and 9.9, 5.15 is 5.16, 8.32 is 8.34, 7.10 is 7.13, 9.21 is 9.23, 12.23 is 12.30, 11.19 is 11.21, 8.52 is 8.54 and 11.7 is the first part of 11.8; 4.4 is the same.

Follows the Greek where Casaubon added to it. 9.21 does not say that I was “made for” a common society; it says that I help to complete a civic whole, so it no longer backs “We are made” in claim 2 and stands with the city picture of claim 1. 5.15 does not say that the best things “are made” for one another; it says that the better are for the sake of one another. 9.7 does not say that people “fly from nature”; it says that they run away and that nature prevails.
Reads body, city, sunlight and soul as four pictures of one claim. Marcus sets sunlight beside soul himself (12.23, 9.7); body and city he never lines up with them.
Joins the return (11.7, 8.32) to 9.7 with “because”. Marcus states the return and credits it to a god (Zeus in 11.7, “god” in 8.32); he does not derive it.
Says “nature” where two of the three passages behind claim 5 name a god: Zeus in 11.7, “god” in 8.32.
articles.limit: Nine of the ten passages feed the article. That is also a risk: fusing smooths over differences. 4.4 argues for the unity step by step, and 9.7 argues from the elements; the article states the unity and keeps neither argument. Ten of the 22 components of its claims rest on two or more passages; the other twelve are one passage’s words.

articles.title: The work that belongs to me

statement.t: My work is to let reason lead in how I treat other people, in how I handle my body, and in how I judge.
statement.form: Three passages each give a list, in different words and at different lengths: 7.30 lists what comes first, second and third in the human make-up, 8.25 what is proper to a human being, and 8.6 the ways in which a rational nature’s road goes well. The statement and the three claims under “In action” come from aligning those lists item by item.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, four of the five claims gain a second author, Practice gains a way to stay my own master amid business, and “When it breaks” gains what Marcus does not say in this section: to look to the intention behind an action and not to its result. To the claim about the body he adds that it may still be indulged.
seneca.statement: The statement stands. Seneca names its ground outright: reason is what is peculiar to a human being.

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: nature bore me as someone who loves all people
piece.follows: I am born to love all human beings.
piece.context: Seneca argues that praise from good men is a good for the man praised; “I” is that good man, glad of it because he loves all people by nature.
gives: mean well by my own kind

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: I do not deny that it should be indulged; I deny that we should be its slaves
piece.follows: The body may be indulged, but we must not be its slaves.
piece.context: On our love of the body, which we must guard; “it” is the body, and the slavery he describes is living for it and fearing on its behalf.
gives: I do not let what it feels rule me

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: we shall still not be partners on equal shares: the mind will take all the rights for itself
piece.follows: While mind and body are joined they are not equal partners: the mind takes all the rights for itself.
piece.context: Seneca refuses to live as his body’s chattel; “partners” are the mind and the body while they are stuck together. A resolve, not a law of nature.
gives: Reason should hold first place

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: And what is it that this reason demands of him? A very easy thing: to live according to his own nature
piece.follows: What reason asks of a human being is to live by his own nature.
piece.context: Seneca has just said a man’s own good is reason perfected in the soul; “his own nature” is the nature of man as a reasoning animal.
gives: living according to my own nature

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: What is peculiar to a human being? Reason: when this is right and brought to its full measure, it has made a human being’s happiness complete.
piece.follows: Reason is what is peculiar to a human being; when it is right and brought to its full measure, his happiness is complete.
piece.context: Each thing is judged by the good that is its own, as a stag by speed; “this” is reason, and he speaks of reason made perfect, not of work under way.
gives: doing it makes me content

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: Because of poverty he is prevented from teaching how the state should be handled, but he teaches this: how poverty should be handled.
piece.follows: Kept by poverty from teaching how a state should be handled, the wise man teaches how poverty should be handled.
piece.context: Seneca answers that hardship cannot stop the wise man as a storm stops a pilot; “he” is the wise man, whom poverty keeps out of public life.
gives: when something blocks one action, dealing with that obstacle becomes my next action

items.label: practice
items.t: I lend myself to my affairs; I do not hand myself over to them.
items.why: Marcus says to hold to the three things and go straight on. Seneca, writing about keeping time for study, says how he stays his own master amid business.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: I do not hand myself over to affairs but lend myself to them
support.follows: I can take part in business without giving myself up to it.
support.context: Seneca denies that business keeps anyone from study; “affairs” are his engagements, and what he keeps back is his time and his own thoughts.

items.label: breaks
items.t: I look to the intention behind what I do, not to how it turns out. The beginning is in my power; fortune decides the outcome.
items.why: Marcus’s claim places the work in the act itself. Seneca adds that the wise man looks to the intention behind an action and not to its result. The article once said this of Marcus too, on Casaubon’s wording of 5.14; the Greek there does not speak of results.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: in everything the wise man looks to the intention, not the outcome. The beginnings are in our power; on the result Fortune passes judgment
support.follows: The wise man looks to the intention behind what he does, not to how it turns out: the start is ours, the outcome is fortune’s.
support.context: Seneca has admitted that a careful life cannot guarantee safety; “the outcome” is how the wise man’s actions turn out, which fortune decides.
gives: I look to the intention behind what I do, not to how it turns out

passages.title: On fame after death and the soul's immortality
passages.text: “Whose good,” he says, “is renown, that is, praise rendered to a good man by good men? Is it the good of the one praised or of the one praising?” Of both. It is mine, as the one who is praised: because nature bore me as someone who loves all people, I both rejoice to have done good and am glad to have found grateful interpreters of the virtues. That they are grateful is a good of several people, but it is mine too. For my mind is so made that I judge the good of others to be mine, at any rate the good of those for whom I am myself the cause of the good.

passages.title: On caring for the body and staying safe
passages.text: I admit that it is planted in us to hold our own body dear; I admit that we hold it in our guardianship. I do not deny that it should be indulged; I deny that we should be its slaves. For the man who is a slave to his body, who fears too much for it, who measures everything by it, will be a slave to many.

passages.title: On causes and the worth of studying nature
passages.text: Never will this flesh drive me to fear, never to a pretence unworthy of a good man; never will I lie to do honour to this little body. When it seems right, I shall break up my partnership with it. And even now, while we are stuck together, we shall still not be partners on equal shares: the mind will take all the rights for itself. Contempt for one’s own body is sure freedom.

passages.title: On the god within us
passages.text: And what is it that this reason demands of him? A very easy thing: to live according to his own nature. But the madness shared by all makes it hard: we push one another into vices. And how can people be called back to health when no one holds them back and the crowd drives them on? Farewell.

passages.title: On learning in old age and the only good
passages.text: What is peculiar to a human being? Reason: when this is right and brought to its full measure, it has made a human being’s happiness complete. So if every thing, when it has perfected its own good, is praiseworthy and has reached the goal of its nature, and if a human being’s own good is reason, then if he has perfected this he is praiseworthy and has touched the goal of his nature. This perfected reason is called virtue, and it is also what is honourable.

passages.title: On rejecting even moderate passions
passages.text: Besides, he is not prevented from being of use even to others at the time when some constraints press on him. Because of poverty he is prevented from teaching how the state should be handled, but he teaches this: how poverty should be handled. His work stretches through the whole of life. So no fortune, no circumstance shuts out the wise man’s actions; for he is busy with the very thing that prevents him from being busy with other things. He is fitted for either turn of events: he steers good things, he conquers bad ones.

passages.title: On making time for study anywhere
passages.text: They are lying, those who want it to look as though a crowd of business stands between them and liberal studies: they feign occupations, they make more of them, and they are the ones who keep themselves occupied. I have time, Lucilius, I have time, and wherever I am, there I am my own. For I do not hand myself over to affairs but lend myself to them, and I do not go hunting for reasons to waste time. And in whatever place I have come to a stop, there I work over my own thoughts and turn something wholesome over in my mind.

passages.title: On caring for the body and staying safe
passages.text: Finally, in everything the wise man looks to the intention, not the outcome. The beginnings are in our power; on the result Fortune passes judgment, and I do not allow her a verdict on me. “But she will bring some harassment, some adversity.” A robber does not condemn when he kills.
