seneca.becomes: With Seneca every claim gains a second author, the empty Practice label gets two exercises, “Why” gets a further argument, and “In action” gains what I may still prefer before a hardship comes. Nothing of Marcus’s is challenged.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement gains a preparation: I accept what happens, and I think ahead to it.

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: These things are decreed; they are not accidents.
piece.follows: Troubles like these are decreed, not accidental.
piece.context: Seneca has just listed his own illness, sick slaves and lost income; “These things” are those troubles, which he calls inevitable.
gives: is not chance

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: the very things by which he seems to be harmed serve to preserve the universe
piece.follows: What seems to harm me serves to preserve the universe.
piece.context: Seneca names the inner defence against Fortune: not chafing at what happens. “The very things” are the events that seem to harm us.
gives: It serves the whole

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: this is how I have been formed: I do not obey god but agree with him
piece.follows: Rather than obey what is decided, I can agree with it.
piece.context: Said of “all the things that seem adverse and hard”; what he agrees with is the illness and losses of 96.1, which Seneca says are decreed.
gives: accept it, and more than accept it

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: Our mind must be fitted to this law; let it follow this, let it obey this; and let it think that whatever happens ought to have happened, and not wish to scold nature.
piece.follows: My mind should be fitted to nature’s law, think that whatever happens ought to have happened, and not scold nature for it.
piece.context: “This law” is nature’s order of changing seasons and opposites, which we cannot alter; “it” is our mind, and “whatever happens” is whatever that order brings.
gives: I shall accept it
fit myself to it

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: None of these things is unusual, none is unexpected.
piece.follows: Setbacks like these are neither unusual nor unexpected.
piece.context: “These things” are Lucilius’s slaves running away; Seneca widens it at once to every knock on life’s journey.
gives: None of it is unusual

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: Whether the fates bind us by an inexorable law, or god, the arbiter of the universe, has arranged everything, or chance drives and tosses human affairs about without order, philosophy ought to protect us.
piece.follows: Even if chance drives everything, philosophy is still my protection.
piece.context: Seneca answers the objection that philosophy is useless if fate, god or chance rules: in each case we need it. The third case is “chance”.
gives: And if nothing governs the world

items.label: why
items.t: And refusing does not spare me: fate leads the willing and drags the unwilling.
items.why: Marcus argues from the good of the whole. This argues that I go either way. Marcus only touches it, in 12.11 (“why do you strain against it?”), which this article uses for something else. Seneca gives the line as Cleanthes’s, in his own Latin.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: The fates lead the willing; the unwilling they drag.
support.follows: Fate takes me along whether I am willing or not.
support.context: The last line of Cleanthes’s prayer to Jupiter, which Seneca puts into Latin to close a letter on following nature’s law; “the willing” and “the unwilling” are anyone at all.
gives: fate leads the willing and drags the unwilling

items.label: practice
items.t: I shall think ahead to everything that can happen, not only to what usually does, so that the blow is lighter when it comes.
items.why: The passages used here give no exercise. Seneca gives this one in three letters. He also warns against overdoing it: in Ep. 13.10 he says not to run out to meet a suffering that has not come.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: the mind must be sent ahead to everything, and what must be thought of is not whatever usually happens but whatever can happen
support.follows: I should think ahead to what can happen, not only to what usually happens.
support.context: Written after fire destroyed Lyons and shook his friend Liberalis; “everything” is whatever Fortune can do, since the unexpected weighs heaviest.
gives: think ahead to everything that can happen, not only to what usually does

support.author: seneca
support.quote: When an evil has been thought out beforehand, its blow comes soft.
support.follows: A misfortune I have already thought about hits less hard.
support.context: Follows a picture of the man who hears of chains and exile calmly; “an evil” is any such threatened hardship, new only to the unprepared.
gives: the blow is lighter when it comes

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Whatever has been long expected is lighter when it comes.
support.follows: What I have long expected is easier when it arrives.
support.context: The closing advice of a letter on illness: keep Fortune’s whole power before your eyes. “Whatever” is any blow she may strike.
gives: the blow is lighter when it comes

items.label: practice
items.t: For a set number of days I shall live on the plainest food and clothing, and ask myself: is this what I was afraid of?
items.why: A second exercise, done with the body and not only in thought. It rehearses a loss before it comes; that is how it bears on accepting what happens.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: set some days in between on which, content with the scantiest and cheapest food and with coarse and rough clothing, you say to yourself, “Is this what was feared?”
support.follows: I should spend set days living poorly and ask myself whether this is what I feared.
support.context: A lesson for the Saturnalia: rehearse poverty while Fortune is kind, so that she cannot catch me off guard. The “this” of the question is being poor.

items.label: doubt
items.t: In that case my stance changes too: a god I follow willingly, but chance I bear, and defy.
items.why: Marcus says only that I can still govern myself. Seneca adds how to stand toward a world run by chance.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: It will urge us to obey god willingly, and Fortune defiantly; it will teach you to follow god and bear chance.
support.follows: Philosophy teaches me to obey a god willingly, and to bear chance and defy it.
support.context: “It” is philosophy, our protection whether fate, god or chance rules; the sentence sets how to stand toward god against how to stand toward Fortune.

items.label: action
items.t: I need not wish for the hardship. I may prefer to be spared it; what I want, if it must be borne, is to bear it with courage.
items.why: Marcus says to be glad of what comes; he does not say what I may wish beforehand. Seneca does. It is not a disagreement: Seneca too is pleased with what has come (Ep. 96.2, 74.20).

support.author: seneca
support.quote: I would want torture to be far from me; but if it has to be endured, I shall wish to carry myself in it bravely, honourably, with spirit.
support.follows: I may prefer not to be tortured; if it must be endured, what I wish for is to bear it with courage.
support.context: Lucilius asked whether brave endurance of torture is a thing to wish for; Seneca answers that the bravery is to be wished for, not the torture.
gives: I may prefer to be spared it; what I want, if it must be borne, is to bear it with courage

support.author: seneca
support.quote: So it is not the hardships that are to be wished for, but the virtue by which the hardships are borne.
support.follows: Hardships are not what is to be wished for; the virtue that lets me bear them is.
support.context: The conclusion Seneca draws from torture, war and illness; “virtue” is brave conduct in them, the only thing there he says is to be wished for.
gives: I need not wish for the hardship

amend.t: , and I prepare for it by thinking ahead to everything that can happen

passages.title: On accepting hardship without complaint
passages.text: These things are decreed; they are not accidents. If you trust me at all, I am at this very moment uncovering my inmost feelings to you: in all the things that seem adverse and hard, this is how I have been formed: I do not obey god but agree with him; I follow him from the heart, not because it is necessary. Nothing will ever befall me that I shall receive gloomily, that I shall receive with a sour face; I shall pay no tax unwillingly. And all the things at which we groan, at which we take fright, are the taxes of life: from these, my Lucilius, do not hope for exemption and do not ask for it.

passages.title: On virtue as the only safe good
passages.text: Let him not be indignant at anything that happens to him, and let him know that the very things by which he seems to be harmed serve to preserve the universe and are among those that bring the course of the world and its task to completion. Let whatever has pleased god please man. For this very reason let him admire himself and what is his: that he cannot be conquered, that he holds evils themselves beneath him, that by reason, and nothing is stronger than reason, he subdues chance and pain and wrong.

passages.title: On accepting fate willingly
passages.text: Our mind must be fitted to this law; let it follow this, let it obey this; and let it think that whatever happens ought to have happened, and not wish to scold nature. It is best to bear what you cannot correct, and, without grumbling, to go along with the god by whose doing all things come about: he is a bad soldier who follows his commander groaning.

passages.title: On accepting fate willingly
passages.text: None of these things is unusual, none is unexpected. To be jolted by such things is as ridiculous as to complain that you are splashed in public or dirtied in the mud. The terms of life are the same as those of a bathhouse, a crowd, a journey: some things will be thrown at you, some will fall on you. Living is not a soft business. You have set out on a long road: you are bound to slip, and knock into things, and fall, and grow tired, and cry out “O death!”, that is, tell a lie. In one place you will leave a companion behind, in another you will carry one out for burial, in another you will be afraid of one. Through jolts of this kind this rough journey has to be travelled to its end.

passages.title: On philosophy as the guide of life
passages.text: Whichever of these is the case, Lucilius, or even if all of them are, one must do philosophy. Whether the fates bind us by an inexorable law, or god, the arbiter of the universe, has arranged everything, or chance drives and tosses human affairs about without order, philosophy ought to protect us. It will urge us to obey god willingly, and Fortune defiantly; it will teach you to follow god and bear chance.

passages.title: On accepting fate willingly
passages.text: Lead me, O father and ruler of the high heaven, wherever you have decided: there is no delay in obeying; I am here, and eager. Suppose I am unwilling: I shall go along groaning, and as a bad man I shall be made to do what I was allowed to do as a good one. The fates lead the willing; the unwilling they drag.

passages.title: On the burning of Lyon and expecting disaster
passages.text: That is why nothing ought to be unforeseen by us; the mind must be sent ahead to everything, and what must be thought of is not whatever usually happens but whatever can happen. For what is there that Fortune, when she has wished it, does not drag down from its fullest flowering? What is there that she does not attack and shake all the more, the more splendidly it shines? What is an uphill climb for her, or what is hard?

passages.title: On learning in old age and the only good
passages.text: When an evil has been thought out beforehand, its blow comes soft. But to fools and to those who trust fortune every face that events show seems new and unexpected; and for the inexperienced a great part of an evil is its newness. So that you may know this: the things they had thought harsh they bear more bravely once they have grown used to them.

passages.title: On bearing illness and pain
passages.text: Meanwhile hold on to this, grip this with your teeth: not to give in to adversity, not to trust prosperity, to keep before your eyes all that Fortune is free to do, as though she were going to do whatever she can do. Whatever has been long expected is lighter when it comes. Farewell.

passages.title: On practising poverty during the holidays
passages.text: But I am so much in favour of testing the firmness of your mind that, following the precept of great men, I shall give a precept to you as well: set some days in between on which, content with the scantiest and cheapest food and with coarse and rough clothing, you say to yourself, “Is this what was feared?”

passages.title: On whether enduring hardship is desirable
passages.text: Draw distinctions among these things, my Lucilius, and you will understand that there is something in them to be wished for. I would want torture to be far from me; but if it has to be endured, I shall wish to carry myself in it bravely, honourably, with spirit. Why would I not prefer that war not break out? But if it does break out, I shall wish to bear wounds, to bear hunger and everything that the necessity of war brings, nobly. I am not so mad as to desire to be ill; but if I have to be ill, I shall wish to do nothing without self-control, nothing womanish. So it is not the hardships that are to be wished for, but the virtue by which the hardships are borne.

claims.role: It comes from one chain of causes
claims.t: What happens to me is not chance alone. All things are linked together, and it comes from a chain of causes, the same that produced me.
claims.shared: Five passages use one family of words: interwoven, interweaving, spun together, fit together, kinship. Two (7.6, 4.36) say that things hold together. Three (10.5, 5.8, 1.17) say that what happens comes through that holding. Only 10.5 says the same causes produced me, and only 1.17 speaks of chance. No passage has the word “chain”: it is the editor’s plain word for the interweaving of causes (10.5) and for what is spun together out of the oldest causes (5.8).
claims.changed: “Not a random blow from outside” is gone: no passage says “from outside”, and 4.36 sets its order against a bare succession, not against chance. 7.6 now backs “linked together”, which is what its “interwoven with one another” says, and no longer “chain of causes”, of which it says nothing. “Not chance” became “not chance alone” when the quotes moved to the project’s English: 1.17 does not deny chance, it says that what comes from chance is not without nature.

support.quote: Whatever happens to you was being made ready for you beforehand, from all time, and the interweaving of causes was spinning together, from eternity, both your existence and the happening of this.
support.follows: The causes that produced me also produced everything that happens to me.
gives: it comes from a chain of causes
the same that produced me

support.quote: it came about for you, and was ordered for you, and stood in some relation to you, spun together from far back out of the oldest causes
support.follows: What happens to me was spun together from far back, out of the oldest causes, and it came about for me.
gives: it comes from a chain of causes

support.quote: All things are interwoven with one another, and the bond is sacred
support.follows: Everything is connected to everything else.
gives: All things are linked together

support.quote: What comes from chance is not without nature, or without the spinning together and interweaving of the things that providence governs.
support.follows: Even what comes from chance is not apart from nature, or from the spinning together and interweaving of the things that providence governs.
gives: is not chance alone
chain of causes

support.quote: just as the things that exist have been arranged to fit together, so the things that come to be show not bare succession but a wonderful kinship
support.follows: The things that exist are arranged to fit together, and in the same way the things that happen do not merely follow one another: they are akin.
gives: All things are linked together

claims.t: It serves the whole of which I am a part. What serves the whole is good for every part, and a part must not complain of it.
claims.shared: Three passages say that what happens is good for the whole (6.40, 5.8) or comes about for its sake (9.38), and two that I am a part of it (1.17, 9.38). Two go on to the part, and each says a different thing: 1.17 that what the nature of the whole brings, and what preserves it, is good for every part; 9.38 that the part must not find fault. They share the subject, not the conclusion.
claims.changed: Was “what serves the whole is not bad for the part”, a middle wording that neither passage says: 1.17 says “good”, and 9.38 speaks of finding fault, not of harm. Each now backs its own words. “Has no reason to complain” became “must not complain” when the quotes moved to the project’s English: 9.38 says the part “must not find fault”, and the Greek has nothing for the 1634 translation’s “against reason”.

support.quote: Whatever happens to each is good for the whole.
support.follows: What happens to any individual is useful to the whole.
gives: It serves the whole

support.quote: it would not bring this to anyone if it did not bring good to the whole
support.follows: Nothing would be brought to anyone if it did not bring good to the whole.
gives: It serves the whole

support.quote: there is besides what is necessary, and what benefits the whole universe, of which you are a part
support.follows: There is also what is necessary and what benefits the whole universe, and I am a part of that universe.
gives: of which I am a part

support.quote: what the nature of the whole brings is good for every part of nature, and so is what preserves that nature
support.follows: Whatever the nature of the whole brings, and whatever preserves that nature, is good for every part.
gives: What serves the whole is good for every part

support.quote: everything happens, one thing upon another, as to one body, from one source that has mind, and the part must not find fault with what comes about for the sake of the whole
support.follows: If everything happens as to one body, from one source that has mind, the part must not find fault with what comes about for the sake of the whole.
gives: of which I am a part
What serves the whole
a part must not complain of it

claims.t: So I shall accept it, and more than accept it: fit myself to it and be glad of it, as I take a harsh prescription for the sake of health.
claims.shared: Four passages give the same instruction with rising warmth: accept, fit yourself, welcome, hold dear, love. Only 5.8 says “accept”; 5.8, 6.39 and 3.17 say “welcome”, which is more. Only 5.8 has Asclepius, the god of healing, and his orders. “So” is Marcus’s own step in 5.8 (“Let us accept these things, then”; “So you should hold dear what falls to you”). “And more than accept it” is the editor’s link and rests on no quote.

support.quote: Let us accept these things, then, as we accept the things Asclepius orders. After all, many of those too are rough, but we welcome them in the hope of health.
support.follows: I should accept what happens as I accept what Asclepius, the god of healing, orders: much of it is rough, and I welcome it in the hope of health.
gives: as I take a harsh prescription for the sake of health
So I shall accept it

support.quote: welcome everything that comes about, even if it seems rather harsh
support.follows: I should welcome everything that comes about, even when it seems harsh.
gives: be glad of it

support.quote: Fit yourself to the things your lot has joined you to
support.follows: I should adapt myself to the circumstances I have been given.
gives: fit myself to it

support.quote: to love and welcome the things that happen to them and are spun together for them
support.follows: The stance named here is to love and welcome the things that happen to me and are spun together for me.
gives: be glad of it
support.note: In 3.17 this is what is left as the good person’s own; that part of the sentence lies outside the quote.

support.quote: one must arrive pure, quiet, ready to be released, fitted to one’s own portion without being forced
support.follows: I must arrive pure, quiet and ready to be released, fitted to my own portion without being forced.
gives: fit myself to it
support.note: In 3.17 the place of arrival is the end of life; those words lie outside the quote.

support.quote: they certainly did deliberate about the affairs of the community, at least, and these things too, which happen as a consequence of those, I ought to welcome and hold dear
support.follows: What happens as a consequence of what the gods deliberated for the community, I ought to welcome and hold dear.
gives: be glad of it

claims.t: None of it is unusual. Sickness, death and slander are as ordinary as roses in spring.
claims.shared: Two passages make what happens familiar and recurring: 4.36 calls it ordinary and familiar, and 9.26 says the cycles of the universe are the same from age to age.

support.quote: Everything that happens is as ordinary and familiar as the rose in spring and fruit in summer.
support.follows: Everything that happens is as ordinary as the seasons.
gives: as ordinary as roses in spring
None of it is unusual

support.quote: illness is like that too, and death, and slander, and plotting
support.follows: Illness, death, slander and plotting are ordinary in the same way.
gives: Sickness, death and slander

support.quote: The cycles of the universe are the same, up and down, from age to age.
support.follows: The cycles of the universe are the same in every age.
gives: None of it is unusual

claims.t: And if nothing governs the world, I still have a reason of my own, and can govern what is mine with it.
claims.shared: Four passages grant the other case, that nothing governs. Three end with something left to me: an order not to act at random myself (9.26), a mind that rules, in myself (12.11), and freedom to deliberate about myself (6.39). Only 12.11 names that mind; the claim calls it reason. 9.38 ends only with “Why, then, are you troubled?”. This is the most repeated move in the section.

support.quote: if it is randomness, do not act at random yourself as well
support.follows: Even if everything is randomness, I must not act at random myself.
gives: And if nothing governs the world
can govern what is mine
support.note: Here Marcus gives only the order not to act at random myself. He does not name reason.

support.quote: if it is a jumble with nothing ruling it, be glad that in such a rough sea you yourself have in yourself a mind that rules
support.follows: Even if the world is a jumble with nothing ruling it, I have in myself a mind that rules, and I can be glad of that.
gives: And if nothing governs the world
I still have a reason of my own
can govern what is mine with it

support.quote: if in fact they deliberate about nothing that concerns us, then I am free to deliberate about myself
support.follows: Even if the gods plan nothing, I may still deliberate about my own affairs.
gives: And if nothing governs the world
can govern what is mine with it

support.quote: there are atoms, and nothing else but a stirred brew and a scattering. Why, then, are you troubled?
support.follows: If there are only atoms, and nothing but a stirred brew and a scattering, there is nothing for me to be troubled about.
gives: And if nothing governs the world
support.note: The question closes both cases, the one body and the atoms. On the atomist case Marcus does not say here that reason remains; he only asks why I am troubled.

single.quote: the complete whole is maimed if you cut through the connection and continuity at any point at all, of its causes just as of its parts. And you do cut through it, as far as it lies with you, whenever you are discontented, and in a way you destroy it.
single.label: A warning
single.t: Each time I am displeased with what happens, I cut through the connection of the whole, as far as lies in me.
single.why: One witness in this section. 8.32, in the section behind Article 1, makes a like point with a severed limb. The quote says only “whenever you are discontented”; that the discontent is with what happens comes from the sentence that opens this argument in 5.8, “you should hold dear what falls to you”, outside the quote.
single.follows: Each time I am discontented I cut through the connection of the whole, as far as it lies with me, and in a way I destroy it.

single.quote: love the people your lot has put you among, but truly
single.label: An addition
single.t: And I shall love the people fate has given me to live with, and love them truly.
single.why: Only 6.35 turns acceptance toward people. It is kept apart for a later article.
single.follows: I should truly love the people my lot has put me among.

members.text:
Up and down, from one age to another, go the ordinary things of
the world; being still the same. And either of everything in particular
before it come to pass, the mind of the universe doth consider with
itself and deliberate: and if so, then submit for shame unto the
determination of such an excellent understanding: or once for all it did
resolve upon all things in general; and since that whatsoever happens,
happens by a necessary consequence, and all things indivisibly in a
manner and inseparably hold one of another. In sum, either there is a
God, and then all is well; or if all things go by chance and fortune,
yet mayest thou use thine own providence in those things that concern
thee properly; and then art thou well.
members.english: The cycles of the universe are the same, up and down, from age to age. And either the mind of the whole has an impulse towards each thing, and if that is so, accept what its impulse is towards; or it had an impulse once, and the rest follows as a consequence, and why do you strain? For in a way: atoms, or things without parts. In sum: if it is god, all is well; if it is randomness, do not act at random yourself as well.
members.greek: Ταὐτά ἐστι τὰ τοῦ κόσμου ἐγκύκλια, ἄνω κάτω, ἐξ αἰῶνος εἰς αἰῶνα. καὶ ἤτοι ἐφ’ ἕκαστον ὁρμᾷ ἡ τοῦ ὅλου διάνοια· ὅπερ εἰ ἔστιν, ἀποδέχου τὸ ἐκείνης ὁρμητόν· ἢ ἅπαξ ὥρμησε, τὰ δὲ λοιπὰ κατ’ ἐπακολούθησιν καὶ τί ἐντείνῃ; τρόπον γάρ τινα ἄτομοι ἢ ἀμερῆ. τὸ δ’ ὅλον, εἴτε θεός, εὖ ἔχει πάντα· εἴτε τὸ εἰκῇ, μὴ καὶ σὺ εἰκῇ.

members.text:
Let not things future trouble thee. For if necessity so require that
they come to pass, thou shalt (whensoever that is) be provided for them
with the same reason, by which whatsoever is now present, is made both
tolerable and acceptable unto thee. All things are linked and knitted
together, and the knot is sacred, neither is there anything in the
world, that is not kind and natural in regard of any other thing, or,
that hath not some kind of reference and natural correspondence with
whatsoever is in the world besides. For all things are ranked together,
and by that decency of its due place and order that each particular
doth observe, they all concur together to the making of one and the same
κόσμος or world: as if you said, a comely piece, or an orderly
composition. For all things throughout, there is but one and the same
order; and through all things, one and the same God, the same substance
and the same law. There is one common reason, and one common truth, that
belongs unto all reasonable creatures, for neither is there save one
perfection of all creatures that are of the same kind, and partakers of
the same reason.
members.english:
Do not let what is to come trouble you. For you will come to it, if you have to, carrying the same reason that you now use on what is present.

All things are interwoven with one another, and the bond is sacred, and hardly anything is foreign to anything else. For they have been arranged together, and together they give order to the same universe. For there is one universe, made of all things, and one god, through all things, and one substance, and one law, the reason common to all living beings that have mind, and one truth, if indeed there is also one perfection for living beings that are of the same kind and share in the same reason.
members.greek:
Τὰ μέλλοντα μὴ ταρασσέτω· ἥξεις γὰρ ἐπ’ αὐτά, ἐὰν δεήσῃ, φέρων τὸν αὐτὸν λόγον ᾧ νῦν πρὸς τὰ παρόντα χρᾷ.

Πάντα ἀλλήλοις ἐπιπλέκεται καὶ ἡ σύνὸεσις ἱερά, καὶ σχεδόν τι οὐδὲν ἀλλότριον ἄλλο ἄλλῳ· συγκατατέτακται γὰρ καὶ συγκοσμεῖ τὸν αὐτὸν κόσμον. κόσμος τε γὰρ εἷς ἐξ ἁπάντων καὶ θεὸς εἷς δι’ ἁπάντων καὶ οὐσία μία καὶ νόμος εἷς, λόγος κοινὸς πάντων τῶν νοερῶν ζῴων καὶ ἀλήθεια μία, εἴγε καὶ τελειότης μία τῶν ὁμογενῶν καὶ τοῦ αὐτοῦ λόγου μετεχόντων ζῴων.

members.text:
As we say commonly, The physician hath prescribed unto this man,
riding; unto another, cold baths; unto a third, to go barefoot: so it
is alike to say, The nature of the universe hath prescribed unto this
man sickness, or blindness, or some loss, or damage or some such thing.
For as there, when we say of a physician, that he hath prescribed
anything, our meaning is, that he hath appointed this for that, as
subordinate and conducing to health: so here, whatsoever doth happen
unto any, is ordained unto him as a thing subordinate unto the fates,
and therefore do we say of such things, that they do συμβαίνειν, that
is, happen, or fall together; as of square stones, when either in
walls, or pyramids in a certain position they fit one another, and
agree as it were in an harmony, the masons say, that they do
συμβαίνειν; as if thou shouldest say, fall together: so that in the
general, though the things be divers that make it, yet the consent or
harmony itself is but one. And as the whole world is made up of all the
particular bodies of the world, one perfect and complete body, of the
same nature that particular bodies; so is the destiny of particular
causes and events one general one, of the same nature that particular
causes are. What I now say, even they that are mere idiots are not
ignorant of: for they say commonly τοῦτο ἔφερεν ἀυτῷ, that is, This
his destiny hath brought upon him. This therefore is by the fates
properly and particularly brought upon this, as that unto this in
particular is by the physician prescribed. These therefore let us
accept of in like manner, as we do those that are prescribed unto us
our physicians. For them also in themselves shall We find to contain
many harsh things, but we nevertheless, in hope of health, and
recovery, accept of them. Let the fulfilling and accomplishment of
those things which the common nature hath determined, be unto thee as
thy health. Accept then, and be pleased with whatsoever doth happen,
though otherwise harsh and un-pleasing, as tending to that end, to the
health and welfare of the universe, and to Jove's happiness and
prosperity. For this whatsoever it be, should not have been produced,
had it not conduced to the good of the universe. For neither doth any
ordinary particular nature bring anything to pass, that is not to
whatsoever is within the sphere of its own proper administration and
government agreeable and subordinate. For these two considerations then
thou must be well pleased with anything that doth happen unto thee.
First, because that for thee properly it was brought to pass, and unto
thee it was prescribed; and that from the very beginning by the series
and connection of the first causes, it hath ever had a reference unto
thee. And secondly, because the good success and perfect welfare, and
indeed the very continuance of Him, that is the Administrator of the
whole, doth in a manner depend on it. For the whole (because whole,
therefore entire and perfect) is maimed, and mutilated, if thou shalt
cut off anything at all, whereby the coherence, and contiguity as of
parts, so of causes, is maintained and preserved. Of which certain it
is, that thou doest (as much as lieth in thee) cut off, and in some
sort violently take somewhat away, as often as thou art displeased with
anything that happeneth.
members.english: When people say, “Asclepius ordered horse-riding for this person, or cold baths, or going barefoot”, it is the same kind of thing as saying, “The nature of the whole ordered an illness for this person, or a maiming, or a loss, or something else of that kind.” For in the first case “ordered” means something like this: he set this in order for this person as suited to health. And in the second, what falls to each person has in some way been set in order for them as suited to fate. For we say that these things “fall” to us in just the way that builders say the squared stones in walls or in pyramids “fall” into place, fitting with one another in a particular arrangement. For in general there is one fitting-together; and just as the universe is made complete, as the body it is, out of all bodies, so fate is made complete, as the cause it is, out of all causes. Even people with no training at all understand what I mean, for they say, “It brought him this.” So then, this was brought to this person, and this was ordered for this person. Let us accept these things, then, as we accept the things Asclepius orders. After all, many of those too are rough, but we welcome them in the hope of health. Let the carrying out and completion of what seems good to the common nature seem to you the same kind of thing as your own health, and so welcome everything that comes about, even if it seems rather harsh, because it leads you there: to the health of the universe, and to the good progress and success of Zeus. For it would not bring this to anyone if it did not bring good to the whole. For not even any ordinary nature brings anything that is not suited to what it governs. So you should hold dear what falls to you, for two reasons. One is that it came about for you, and was ordered for you, and stood in some relation to you, spun together from far back out of the oldest causes. The other is that what comes to each person individually is also a cause, for the one that governs the whole, of good progress and of completion and, by Zeus, of continuance itself. For the complete whole is maimed if you cut through the connection and continuity at any point at all, of its causes just as of its parts. And you do cut through it, as far as it lies with you, whenever you are discontented, and in a way you destroy it.
members.greek: Ὁποῖόν τί ἐστι τὸ λεγόμενον, ὅτι· συνέταξεν ὁ Ἀσκληπιὸς τούτῳ ἱππασίαν ἢ ψυχρολουσίαν ἢ ἀνυποδησίαν, τοιοῦτόν ἐστι καὶ τό· συνέταξε τούτῳ ἡ τῶν ὅλων φύσις νόσον ἢ πήρωσιν ἢ ἀποβολὴν ἢ ἄλλο τι τῶν τοιούτων. καὶ γὰρ ἐκεῖ τὸ συνέταξε τοιοῦτόν τι σημαίνει· ἔταξε τούτῳ τοῦτο ὡς κατάλληλον πρὸς ὑγίειαν, καὶ ἐνταῦθα τὸ συμβαῖνον ἑκάστῳ τέτακταί πως αὐτῷ ὡς κατάλληλον πρὸς τὴν εἱμαρμένην. οὕτως γὰρ καὶ συμβαίνειν αὐτὰ ἡμῖν λέγομεν ὡς καὶ τοὺς τετραγώνους λίθους ἐν τοῖς τείχεσιν ἤ ἐν ταῖς πυραμίσι συμβαίνειν οἱ τεχνῖται λέγουσι, συναρμόζοντας ἀλλήλοις τῇ ποιᾷ συνθέσει. ὅλως γὰρ ἁρμονία ἐστὶ μία καὶ ὥσπερ ἐκ πάντων τῶν σωμάτων ὁ κόσμος τοιοῦτον σῶμα συμπληροῦται, οὕτως ἐκ πάντων τῶν αἰτίων ἡ εἱμαρμένη τοιαύτη αἰτία συμπληροῦται. νοοῦσι δὲ ὃ λέγω καὶ οἱ τέλεον ἰδιῶται· φασὶ γάρ· τοῦτο ἔφερεν αὐτῷ. οὐκοῦν τοῦτο τούτῳ ἐφέρετο καὶ τοῦτο τούτῳ συνετάττετο· δεχώμεθα οὖν αὐτὰ ὡς ἐκεῖνα ἃ ὁ Ἀσκληπιὸς συντάττει. πολλὰ γοῦν καὶ ἐν ἐκείνοις ἐστὶ τραχέα, ἀλλὰ ἀσπαζόμεθα τῇ ἐλπίδι τῆς ὑγιείας. τοιοῦτόν τί σοι δοκείτω ἄνυσις καὶ συντέλεια τῶν τῇ κοινῇ φύσει δοκούντων, οἷον ἡ σὴ ὑγίεια, καὶ οὕτως ἀσπάζου πᾶν τὸ γινόμενον, κἂν ἀπηνέστερον δοκῇ, διὰ τὸ ἐκεῖ σε ἄγειν, ἐπὶ τὴν τοῦ κόσμου ὑγίειαν καὶ τὴν τοῦ Διὸς εὐοδίαν καὶ εὐπραγίαν. οὐ γὰρ ἂν τοῦτό τινι ἔφερεν, εἰ μὴ τῷ ὅλῳ συνέφερεν· οὐδὲ γὰρ ἡ τυχοῦσα φύσις φέρει τι, ὃ μὴ τῷ διοικουμένῳ ὑπ’ αὐτῆς κατάλληλόν ἐστιν. οὐκοῦν κατὰ δύο λόγους στέργειν χρὴ τὸ συμβαῖνόν σοι· καθ’ ἕνα μέν, ὅτι σοὶ ἐγίνετο καὶ σοὶ συνετάττετο καὶ πρὸς σέ πως εἶχεν, ἄνωθεν ἐκ τῶν πρεσβυτάτων αἰτίων συγκλωθόμενον· καθ’ ἕτερον δέ, ὅτι τῷ τὸ ὅλον διοικοῦντι τῆς εὐοδίας καὶ τῆς συντελείας καὶ νὴ Δία τῆς συμμονῆς αὐτῆς καὶ τὸ ἰδίᾳ εἰς ἕκαστον ἧκον αἴτιόν ἐστι. πηροῦται γὰρ τὸ ὁλόκληρον, ἐὰν καὶ ὁτιοῦν διακόψῃς τῆς συναφείας καὶ συνεχείας ὥσπερ τῶν μορίων, οὕτω δὴ καὶ τῶν αἰτίων· διακόπτεις δέ, ὅσον ἐπὶ σοί, ὅταν δυσαρεστῇς, καὶ τρόπον τινὰ ἀναιρεῖς.

members.text:
Whatsoever proceeds from the gods immediately, that any man will
grant totally depends from their divine providence. As for those
things that are commonly said to happen by fortune, even those must be
conceived to have dependence from nature, or from that first and general
connection, and concatenation of all those things, which more apparently
by the divine providence are administered and brought to pass.
All things flow from thence: and whatsoever it is that is, is both
necessary, and conducing to the whole (part of which thou art), and
whatsoever it is that is requisite and necessary for the preservation of
the general, must of necessity for every particular nature, be good and
behoveful. And as for the whole, it is preserved, as by the perpetual
mutation and conversion of the simple elements one into another, so
also by the mutation, and alteration of things mixed and compounded. Let
these things suffice thee; let them be always unto thee, as thy general
rules and precepts. As for thy thirst after books, away with it with all
speed, that thou die not murmuring and complaining, but truly meek and
well satisfied, and from thy heart thankful unto the gods.
members.english: What comes from the gods is full of providence. What comes from chance is not without nature, or without the spinning together and interweaving of the things that providence governs. Everything flows from there. And there is besides what is necessary, and what benefits the whole universe, of which you are a part. And what the nature of the whole brings is good for every part of nature, and so is what preserves that nature. And the universe is preserved by changes: those of the elements and, in the same way, those of compound things. Let this be enough for you, and let these be your principles. As for your thirst for books, throw it away, so that you do not die grumbling, but truly gracious, and thankful to the gods from your heart.
members.greek: Τὰ τῶν θεῶν προνοίας μεστά. τὰ τῆς τύχης οὐκ ἄνευ φύσεως ἢ συγκλώσεως καὶ ἐπιπλοκῆς τῶν προνοίᾳ διοικουμένων. πάντα ἐκεῖθεν ῥεῖ· πρόσεστι δὲ τὸ ἀναγκαῖον καὶ τὸ τῷ ὅλῳ κόσμῳ συμφέρον, οὗ μέρος εἶ. παντὶ δὲ φύσεως μέρει ἀγαθόν, ὃ φέρει ἡ τοῦ ὅλου φύσις καὶ ὃ ἐκείνης ἐστὶ σωστικόν. σῴζουσι δὲ κόσμον, ὥσπερ αἱ τῶν στοιχείων, οὕτως καὶ αἱ τῶν συγκριμάτων μεταβολαί. ταῦτά σοι ἀρκείτω καὶ δόγματα ἔστω. τὴν δὲ τῶν βιβλίων δίψαν ῥῖψον, ἵνα μὴ γογγύζων ἀποθάνῃς, ἀλλὰ ἵλεως ἀληθῶς καὶ ἀπὸ καρδίας εὐχάριστος τοῖς θεοῖς.

members.text:
Fit and accommodate thyself to that estate and to those
occurrences, which by the destinies have been annexed unto thee; and
love those men whom thy fate it is to live with; but love them truly. An
instrument, a tool, an utensil, whatsoever it be, if it be fit for the
purpose it was made for, it is as it should be though he perchance that
made and fitted it, be out of sight and gone. But in things natural,
that power which hath framed and fitted them, is and abideth within them
still: for which reason she ought also the more to be respected, and we
are the more obliged (if we may live and pass our time according to her
purpose and intention) to think that all is well with us, and according
to our own minds. After this manner also, and in this respect it is,
that he that is all in all doth enjoy his happiness.
members.english:
Fit yourself to the things your lot has joined you to, and love the people your lot has put you among, but truly.

Every instrument, tool or utensil is as it should be if it does what it was made for; and yet in that case the one who made it is away. But in things held together by nature, the power that made them is inside and stays there. For that reason you should respect it all the more, and consider that if you keep to its will and live by it, everything is as your mind would have it. And in the same way, for the All too, what is its own is as its mind would have it.
members.greek:
Οἷς συγκεκλήρωσαι πράγμασι, τούτοις συνάρμοζε σεαυτὸν καὶ οἷς συνείληχας ἀνθρώποις, τούτους φίλει, ἀλλ’ ἀληθινῶς.

Ὄργανον, ἐργαλεῖον, σκεῦος πᾶν εἰ πρὸς ὃ κατεσκεύασται ποιεῖ, εὖ ἔχει· καίτοι ἐκεῖ ὁ κατασκευάσας ἐκποδών. ἐπὶ δὲ τῶν ὑπὸ φύσεως συνεχομένων ἔνδον ἐστὶ καὶ παραμένει ἡ κατασκευάσοσα δύναμις· καθὸ καὶ μᾶλλον αἰδεῖσθαι αὐτὴν δεῖ καὶ νομίζειν, ἐὰν κατὰ τὸ βούλημα ταύτης ἔχῃς καὶ διεξάγῃς, ἔχειν σοι πάντα κατὰ νοῦν. ἔχει δὲ οὕτως καὶ τῷ παντὶ κατὰ νοῦν τὰ ἑαυτοῦ.

members.why: A list of reminders about convention, death, pain and fame. Too many subjects to fuse with anything here.
members.text:
All things (saith he) are by certain order and appointment. And
what if the elements only.

It will suffice to remember, that all things in general are by certain
order and appointment: or if it be but few. And as concerning death,
that either dispersion, or the atoms, or annihilation, or extinction,
or translation will ensue. And as concerning pain, that that which is
intolerable is soon ended by death; and that which holds long must needs
be tolerable; and that the mind in the meantime (which is all in all)
may by way of interclusion, or interception, by stopping all manner of
commerce and sympathy with the body, still retain its own tranquillity.
Thy understanding is not made worse by it. As for those parts that
suffer, let them, if they can, declare their grief themselves. As for
praise and commendation, view their mind and understanding, what estate
they are in; what kind of things they fly, and what things they seek
after: and that as in the seaside, whatsoever was before to be seen,
is by the continual succession of new heaps of sand cast up one upon
another, soon hid and covered; so in this life, all former things by
those which immediately succeed.
members.english:
He says, “All things are by convention, and in reality only the elements.” But it is enough to remember that all things are by convention. Already very few.

On death: either a scattering, if there are atoms; or, if there is a unity, either a snuffing out or a move elsewhere.

On pain: what cannot be borne carries one off, and what lasts can be borne. And the mind keeps its own calm by separation, and the ruling part has not become worse. As for the parts that are harmed by the pain, let them give their verdict on it, if they can.

On fame: look at their minds, what they are like, and what kind of things they run from and what kind of things they chase. And see that, as heaps of sand piled one on another hide the earlier ones, so in life the earlier things are very quickly covered by those piled on after.
members.greek:
ἐκεῖνος μέν φησιν ὅτι ʽπάντα νομιστί, ἐτεῇ δὲ μόνα τὰ στοιχεῖαʼ, ἀρκεῖ δὲ μεμνῆσθαι ὅτι τὰ πάντα νομιστὶ ἔχει· ἤδη λίαν ὀλίγα.

Περὶ θανάτου· ἢ σκεδασμός, εἰ ἄτομοι· εἰ δ᾽ ἕνωσις, ἤτοι σβέσις ἢ μετάστασις.

Περὶ πόνου· τὸ μὲν ἀφόρητον ἐξάγει, τὸ δὲ χρονίζον φορητόν· καὶ ἡ διάνοια τὴν ἑαυτῆς γαλήνην κατὰ ἀπόληψιν διατηρεῖ καὶ οὐ χεῖρον τὸ ἡγεμονικὸν γέγονε, τὰ δὲ κακούμενα μέρη ὑπὸ τοῦ πόνου, εἴ τι δύναται, περὶ αὐτοῦ ἀποφηνάσθω.

Περὶ δόξης· ἴδε τὰς διανοίας αὐτῶν, οἷαι καὶ οἷα μὲν φεύγουσαι. οἷα δὲ διώκουσαι. καὶ ὅτι, ὡς αἱ θῖνες ἄλλαι ἐπ’ ἄλλαις ἐπιφορούμεναι κρύπτουσι τὰς προτέρας, οὕτως ἐν τῷ βίῳ τὰ πρότερα ὑπὸ τῶν ἐπενεχθέντων τάχιστα ἐκαλύφθη.

members.why: Questions to ask of any impression, tracing each thing to god, to the shared lot and chance, or to a kinsman. An exercise in examining impressions, nearer to judgment than to accepting what happens.
members.text:
What is this, that now my fancy is set upon? of what things doth
it consist? how long can it last? which of all the virtues is the proper
virtue for this present use? as whether meekness, fortitude, truth,
faith, sincerity, contentation, or any of the rest? Of everything
therefore thou must use thyself to say, This immediately comes from God,
this by that fatal connection, and concatenation of things, or (which
almost comes to one) by some coincidental casualty. And as for this, it
proceeds from my neighbour, my kinsman, my fellow: through his ignorance
indeed, because he knows not what is truly natural unto him: but I know
it, and therefore carry myself towards him according to the natural law
of fellowship; that is kindly, and justly. As for those things that of
themselves are altogether indifferent, as in my best judgment I conceive
everything to deserve more or less, so I carry myself towards it.
members.english: What is it, and what is it compounded of, and how long is it in its nature to last, this thing that is now making the impression on me? And what virtue is needed for it: gentleness, for example, courage, good faith, simplicity, self-sufficiency, and the rest? So in each case one must say: this comes from god; this comes by the shared lot, and the spinning and winding together, and this kind of coincidence and chance; and this comes from one of my own tribe, a kinsman and partner, who does not know, however, what is in accordance with nature for them. But I do know. That is why I treat them according to the natural law of partnership, with good will and justly; and yet at the same time, in things that are neither good nor bad, I aim at what accords with worth.
members.greek: τί ἐστὶ καὶ ἐκ τίνων συγκέκριται καὶ πόσον χρόνον πέφυκε παραμένειν τοῦτο τὸ τὴν φαντασίαν μοι νῦν ποιοῦν καὶ τίνος ἀρετῆς πρὸς αὐτὸ χρεία, οἷον ἡμερότητος, ἀνδρείας, πίστεως, ἀφελείας, αὐταρκείας, τῶν λοιπῶν. διὸ δεῖ ἐφ̓ ἑκάστου λέγειν· τοῦτο μὲν παρὰ θεοῦ ἥκει, τοῦτο δὲ κατὰ τὴν σύλληξιν καὶ τὴν συμμηρυομένην σύγκλωσιν καὶ τὴν τοιαύτην σύντευξίν τε καὶ τύχην, τοῦτο δὲ παρὰ τοῦ συμφύλου καὶ συγγενοῦς καὶ κοινωνοῦ, ἀγνοοῦντος μέντοι ὅ τι αὐτῷ κατὰ φύσιν ἐστίν. ἀλλ’ ἐγὼ οὐκ ἀγνοῶ· διὰ τοῦτο χρῶμαι αὐτῷ κατὰ τὸν τῆς κοινωνίας φυσικὸν νόμον εὔνως καὶ δικαίως, ἅμα μέντοι τοῦ κατ’ ἀξίαν ἐν τοῖς μέσοις συστοχάζομαι.

members.text:
Whatsoever doth happen in the world, is, in the course of nature,
as usual and ordinary as a rose in the spring, and fruit in summer. Of
the same nature is sickness and death; slander, and lying in wait, and
whatsoever else ordinarily doth unto fools use to be occasion either
of joy or sorrow. That, whatsoever it is, that comes after, doth always
very naturally, and as it were familiarly, follow upon that which was
before. For thou must consider the things of the world, not as a loose
independent number, consisting merely of necessary events; but as a
discreet connection of things orderly and harmoniously disposed. There
is then to be seen in the things of the world, not a bare succession,
but an admirable correspondence and affinity.
members.english:
Everything that happens is as ordinary and familiar as the rose in spring and fruit in summer. For illness is like that too, and death, and slander, and plotting, and all the things that gladden or grieve fools.

What comes next always follows what went before as kin to it. For it is not like a counting-off of separate items that has only compulsion in it, but a connection that has reason in it. And just as the things that exist have been arranged to fit together, so the things that come to be show not bare succession but a wonderful kinship.
members.greek:
Πᾶν τὸ συμβαῖνον οὕτως σύνηθες καὶ γνώριμον ὡς τὸ ῥόδον ἐν τῷ ἔαρι καὶ ὀπώρα ἐν τῷ θέρει· τοιοῦτον γὰρ καὶ νόσος καὶ θάνατος καὶ βλασφημία καὶ ἐπιβουλὴ καὶ ὅσα τοὺς μωροὺς εὐφραίνει ἣ λυπεῖ.

Τὰ ἑξῆς ἀεὶ τοῖς προηγησαμένοις οἰκείως ἐπιγίνεται· οὐ γὰρ οἷον καταρίθμησίς τίς ἐστιν ἀπηρτημένως καὶ μόνον τὸ κατηναγκασμένον ἔχουσα, ἀλλὰ συνάφεια εὔλογος καὶ ὥσπερ συντέτακται συνηρμοσμένως τὰ ὄντα, οὕτως τὰ γινόμενα οὐ διαδοχὴν ψιλήν, ἀλλὰ θαυμαστήν τινα οἰκειότητα ἐμφαίνει.

members.text:
Either fate, (and that either an absolute necessity, and unavoidable
decree; or a placable and flexible Providence) or all is a mere
casual confusion, void of all order and government. If an absolute and
unavoidable necessity, why doest thou resist? If a placable and exorable
Providence, make thyself worthy of the divine help and assistance. If
all be a mere confusion without any moderator, or governor, then hast
thou reason to congratulate thyself; that in such a general flood of
confusion thou thyself hast obtained a reasonable faculty, whereby thou
mayest govern thine own life and actions. But if thou beest carried
away with the flood, it must be thy body perchance, or thy life, or some
other thing that belongs unto them that is carried away: thy mind and
understanding cannot. Or should it be so, that the light of a candle
indeed is still bright and lightsome until it be put out: and should
truth, and righteousness, and temperance cease to shine in thee whilest
thou thyself hast any being?
members.english:
Either a necessity of fate and an order that cannot be overstepped, or a providence that can be appeased, or a jumble of randomness with no one in charge. If, then, it is a necessity that cannot be overstepped, why do you strain against it? If it is a providence that allows itself to be appeased, make yourself worthy of the help that comes from the divine. And if it is a jumble with nothing ruling it, be glad that in such a rough sea you yourself have in yourself a mind that rules. And if the sea carries you away, let it carry away the poor flesh, the bit of breath, the rest; for the mind it will not carry away.

Or does the light of a lamp shine until it goes out, and not lose its brightness, while the truth and justice and self-control in you will go out first?
members.greek:
Ἤτοι ἀνάγκη εἱμαρμένης καὶ ἀπαράβατος τάξις ἢ πρόνοια ἱλάσιμος ἢ φυρμὸς εἰκαιότητος ἀπροστάτητος. εἰ μὲν οὖν ἀπαράβατος ἀνάγκη, τί ἀντιτείνεις; εἰ δὲ πρόνοια ἐπιδεχομένη τὸ ἱλάσκεσθαι, ἄξιον σαυτὸν ποίησον τῆς ἐκ τοῦ θείου βοηθείας. εἰ δὲ φυρμὸς ἀνηγεμόνευτος, ἀσμένιζε ὅτι ἐν τοιούτῳ κλύδωνι αὐτὸς ἔχεις ἐν σαυτῷ τινα νοῦν ἡγεμονικόν, κἂν παραφέρῃ σε ὁ κλύδων, παραφερέτω τὸ σαρκίδιον, τὸ πνευμάτιον, τἄλλα· τὸν γὰρ νοῦν οὐ παροίσει.

ἢ τὸ μὲν τοῦ λύχνου φῶς, μέχρι σβεσθῇ, φαίνει καὶ τὴν αὐγὴν οὐκ ἀποβάλλει· ἡ δὲ ἐν σοὶ ἀλήθεια καὶ δικαιοσύνη καὶ σωφροσύνη προαποσβήσεται;

members.text:
If so be that the Gods have deliberated in particular of those
things that should happen unto me, I must stand to their deliberation,
as discrete and wise. For that a God should be an imprudent God, is a
thing hard even to conceive: and why should they resolve to do me hurt?
for what profit either unto them or the universe (which they specially
take care for) could arise from it? But if so be that they have not
deliberated of me in particular, certainly they have of the whole in
general, and those things which in consequence and coherence of this
general deliberation happen unto me in particular, I am bound to embrace
and accept of. But if so be that they have not deliberated at all (which
indeed is very irreligious for any man to believe: for then let us
neither sacrifice, nor pray, nor respect our oaths, neither let us any
more use any of those things, which we persuaded of the presence and
secret conversation of the Gods among us, daily use and practise:)
but, I say, if so be that they have not indeed either in general, or
particular deliberated of any of those things, that happen unto us
in this world; yet God be thanked, that of those things that
concern myself, it is lawful for me to deliberate myself, and all my
deliberation is but concerning that which may be to me most profitable.
Now that unto every one is most profitable, which is according to his
own constitution and nature. And my nature is, to be rational in all my
actions and as a good, and natural member of a city and commonwealth,
towards my fellow members ever to be sociably and kindly disposed and
affected. My city and country as I am Antoninus, is Rome; as a man, the
whole world. Those things therefore that are expedient and profitable to
those cities, are the only things that are good and expedient for me.
members.english: If, then, the gods deliberated about me and about the things that had to happen to me, they deliberated well. For a god without deliberation is not easy even to imagine; and for what cause would they have had an impulse to do me harm? For what would they, or the community, which is what they take most thought for, have gained from it? But if they did not deliberate about me individually, they certainly did deliberate about the affairs of the community, at least, and these things too, which happen as a consequence of those, I ought to welcome and hold dear. But if in fact they deliberate about nothing (to believe that is not pious; or else let us not sacrifice, or pray, or swear oaths, or do the other things that we do at every turn towards the gods as present and living with us), if in fact they deliberate about nothing that concerns us, then I am free to deliberate about myself, and my inquiry is into what is of benefit. What benefits each is what accords with its own make-up and nature, and my nature is rational and civic. My city and fatherland, as Antoninus, is Rome; as a human being, the universe. So the things that are useful to these cities are the only things that are good for me.
members.greek: Εἰ μὲν οὖν ἐβουλεύσαντο περὶ ἐμοῦ καὶ τῶν ἐμοὶ συμβῆναι ὀφειλόντων οἱ θεοί, καλῶς ἐβουλεύσαντο· ἄβουλον γὰρ θεὸν οὐδὲ ἐπινοῆσαι ῥᾴδιον, κακοποιῆσαι δέ με διὰ τίνα αἰτίαν ἔμελλον ὁρμᾶν; τί γὰρ αὐτοῖς ἢ τῷ κοινῷ, οὗ μάλιστα προνοοῦνται, ἐκ τούτου περιεγένετο; εἰ δὲ μὴ ἐβουλεύσαντο κατ’ ἰδίαν περὶ ἐμοῦ, περί γε τῶν κοινῶν πάντως ἐβουλεύσαντο, οἷς κατ’ ἐπακολούθησιν καὶ ταῦτα συμβαίνοντα ἀσπάζεσθαι καὶ στέργειν ὀφείλω. εἰ δʼ ἄρα περὶ μηδενὸς βουλεύονται (πιστεύειν μὲν οὐχ ὅσιον ἢ μηδὲ θύωμεν μηδὲ εὐχώμεθα μηδὲ ὀμνύωμεν μηδὲ τὰ ἄλλα πράσσωμεν ἃ παρ’ ἕκαστα ὡς πρὸς παρόντας καὶ συμβιοῦντας τοὺς θεοὺς πράσσομεν), εἰ δ’ ἄρα περὶ μηδενὸς τῶν καθ’ ἡμᾶς βουλεύονται, ἐμοὶ μὲν ἔξεστι περὶ ἐμαυτοῦ βουλεύεσθαι, ἐμοὶ δέ ἐστι σκέψις περὶ τοῦ συμφέροντος. συμφέρει δὲ ἑκάστῳ τὸ κατὰ τὴν ἑαυτοῦ κατασκευὴν καὶ φύσιν, ἡ δὲ ἐμὴ φύσις λογικὴ καὶ πολιτική. Πόλις καὶ πατρὶς ὡς μὲν Ἀντωνίνῳ μοι ἡ Ῥώμη, ὡς δὲ ἀνθρώπῳ ὁ κόσμος. τὰ ταῖς πόλεσιν οὖν ταύταις ὠφέλιμα μόνα ἐστί μοι ἀγαθά.

members.why: What happens, happens justly. A stronger claim than claim 2, and only this passage makes it.
members.text:
Whatsoever doth happen in the world, doth happen justly, and so if
thou dost well take heed, thou shalt find it. I say not only in right
order by a series of inevitable consequences, but according to justice
and as it were by way of equal distribution, according to the true worth
of everything. Continue then to take notice of it, as thou hast begun,
and whatsoever thou dost, do it not without this proviso, that it be a
thing of that nature that a good man (as the word good is properly
taken) may do it. This observe carefully in every action.
members.english: That “everything that happens, happens justly”. If you watch closely, you will find it so. I do not mean only according to the order in which one thing follows another, but that it is according to what is just, and as if by someone handing out what accords with worth. So keep watching, as you have begun, and whatever you do, do it with this: with being good, in the sense in which the good person is properly understood. Keep this in every action.
members.greek: Ὅτι “πᾶν τὸ συμβαῖνον δικαίως συμβαίνει” · ὃ ἐὰν ἀκριβῶς παραφυλάσσῃς, εὑρήσεις· οὐ λέγω μόνον κατὰ τὸ ἑξῆς, ἀλλʼ ὅτι κατὰ τὸ δίκαιον καὶ ὡς ἂν ὑπό τινος ἀπονέμοντος τὸ κατʼ ἀξίαν. παραφύλασσε οὖν ὡς ἤρξω, καί, ὅ τι ἂν ποιῇς, σὺν τούτῳ ποίει, σὺν τῷ ἀγαθὸς εἶναι, καθὸ νενόηται ἰδίως ὁ ἀγαθός. τοῦτο ἐπὶ πάσης ἐνεργείας σῷζε.

members.text:
To be capable of fancies and imaginations, is common to man and
beast. To be violently drawn and moved by the lusts and desires of the
soul, is proper to wild beasts and monsters, such as Phalaris and Nero
were. To follow reason for ordinary duties and actions is common to them
also, who believe not that there be any gods, and for their advantage
would make no conscience to betray their own country; and who when once
the doors be shut upon them, dare do anything. If therefore all things
else be common to these likewise, it follows, that for a man to like and
embrace all things that happen and are destinated unto him, and not to
trouble and molest that spirit which is seated in the temple of his own
breast, with a multitude of vain fancies and imaginations, but to keep
him propitious and to obey him as a god, never either speaking anything
contrary to truth, or doing anything contrary to justice, is the only
true property of a good man. And such a one, though no man should
believe that he liveth as he doth, either sincerely and conscionably,
or cheerful and contentedly; yet is he neither with any man at all angry
for it, nor diverted by it from the way that leadeth to the end of his
life, through which a man must pass pure, ever ready to depart, and
willing of himself without any compulsion to fit and accommodate himself
to his proper lot and portion.
members.english: To be stamped with impressions belongs to cattle as well. To be pulled by the strings of impulse belongs also to wild beasts, and to effeminate men, and to Phalaris and Nero. And to have the mind as leader towards what appear to be the fitting things to do belongs also to those who do not believe in gods, and those who desert their country, and those who do what they do once they have shut the doors. If, then, the rest is shared with those just mentioned, what is left as the good person’s own is to love and welcome the things that happen to them and are spun together for them; and not to muddy the spirit seated within the chest, nor disturb it with a crowd of impressions, but to keep it gracious, following god in good order, neither saying anything contrary to what is true nor doing anything contrary to what is just. And if all people disbelieve that the good person lives simply and modestly and cheerfully, the good person is not angry with any of them, and is not turned aside from the road that leads to the end of life, at which one must arrive pure, quiet, ready to be released, fitted to one’s own portion without being forced.
members.greek: τὸ μὲν τυποῦσθαι φανταστικῶς καὶ τῶν βοσκημάτων· τὸ δὲ νευροσπαστεῖσθαι ὁρμητικῶς καὶ τῶν θηρίων καὶ τῶν ἀνδρογύνων καὶ Φαλάριδος καὶ Νέρωνος· τὸ δὲ τὸν νοῦν ἡγεμόνα ἔχειν ἐπὶ τὰ φαινόμενα καθήκοντα καὶ τῶν θεοὺς μὴ νομιζόντων καὶ τῶν τὴν πατρίδα ἐγκαταλειπόντων καὶ τῶν ποιούντων, ἐπειδὰν κλείσωσι τὰς θύρας. εἰ οὖν τὰ λοιπὰ κοινά ἐστι πρὸς τὰ εἰρημένα, λοιπὸν τὸ ἴδιόν ἐστι τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ φιλεῖν μὲν καὶ ἀσπάζεσθαι τὰ συμβαίνοντα καὶ συγκλωθόμενα αὐτῷ, τὸν δὲ ἔνδον ἐν τῷ στήθει ἱδρυμένον δαίμονα μὴ φύρειν μηδὲ θορυβεῖν ὄχλῳ φαντασιῶν, ἀλλὰ ἵλεων διατηρεῖν, κοσμίως ἑπόμενον θεῷ, μήτε φθεγγόμενόν τι παρὰ τὰ ἀληθῆ μήτε ἐνεργοῦντα παρὰ τὰ δίκαια. εἰ δὲ ἀπιστοῦσιν αὐτῷ πάντες ἄνθρωποι, ὅτι ἁπλῶς καὶ αἰδημόνως καὶ εὐθύμως βιοῖ, οὔτε χαλεπαίνει τινὶ τούτων οὔτε παρατρέπεται τῆς ὁδοῦ τῆς ἀγούσης ἐπὶ τὸ τέλος τοῦ βίου, ἐφ’ ὃ δεῖ ἐλθεῖν καθαρόν, ἡσύχιον, εὔλυτον, ἀβιάστως τῇ ἑαυτοῦ μοίρᾳ συνηρμοσμένον.

members.text:
Either all things by the providence of reason happen unto every
particular, as a part of one general body; and then it is against reason
that a part should complain of anything that happens for the good of the
whole; or if, according to Epicurus, atoms be the cause of all things
and that life be nothing else but an accidentary confusion of things,
and death nothing else, but a mere dispersion and so of all other
things: what doest thou trouble thyself for?
members.english: Either everything happens, one thing upon another, as to one body, from one source that has mind, and the part must not find fault with what comes about for the sake of the whole; or there are atoms, and nothing else but a stirred brew and a scattering. Why, then, are you troubled?
members.greek: Ἤτοι ἀπὸ μιᾶς πηγῆς νοερᾶς πάντα ὡς ἑνὶ σώματι ἐπισυμβαίνει καὶ οὐ δεῖ τὸ μέρος τοῖς ὑπὲρ τοῦ ὅλου γινομένοις μέμφεσθαι· ἢ ἄτομοι καὶ οὐδὲν ἄλλο ἢ κυκεὼν καὶ σκεδασμός· τί οὖν ταράσσῃ;

members.text:
Whatsoever it be that happens unto thee, it is that which from all
time was appointed unto thee. For by the same coherence of causes, by
which thy substance from all eternity was appointed to be, was also
whatsoever should happen unto it, destinated and appointed.
members.english: Whatever happens to you was being made ready for you beforehand, from all time, and the interweaving of causes was spinning together, from eternity, both your existence and the happening of this.
members.greek: Ὅ τι ἄν σοι συμβαίνῃ, τοῦτό σοι ἐξ αἰῶνος προκατεσκευάζετο καὶ ἡ ἐπιπλοκὴ τῶν αἰτίων συνέκλωθε τήν τε σὴν ὑπόστασιν ἐξ ἀιδίου καὶ τὴν τούτου σύμβασιν.

members.text:
Whatsoever in any kind doth happen to any one, is expedient to the
whole. And thus much to content us might suffice, that it is expedient
for the whole in general. But yet this also shalt thou generally
perceive, if thou dost diligently take heed, that whatsoever doth happen
to any one man or men.... And now I am content that the word expedient,
should more generally be understood of those things which we otherwise
call middle things, or things indifferent; as health, wealth, and the
like.
members.english: Whatever happens to each is good for the whole. That would be enough. But if you watch you will also see this, as a general rule: whatever happens to one person is good for other people too. Here, though, let “good for” be taken in the more ordinary sense, as applied to things that are neither good nor bad.
members.greek: Ὅσα ἑκάστῳ συμβαίνει, ταῦτα τῷ ὅλῳ συμφέρει· ἤρκει τοῦτο. ἀλλ’ ἔτι ἐκεῖνο ὡς ἐπίπαν ὄψει παραφυλάξας, ὅσα ἀνθρώπῳ, καὶ ἑτέροις ἀνθρώποις. κοινότερον δὲ νῦν τὸ συμφέρον ἐπὶ τῶν μέσων λαμβανέσθω.

decisions: Presents the section as one argument by cases. Marcus gives the cases in four passages and never the whole chain in one place.

Keeps apart the two things said about the part: 1.17 says that what the nature of the whole brings, and what preserves it, is good for every part; 9.38 says that the part must not find fault. An earlier draft merged them into “not bad for the part”, which neither says.

Records no editor’s inference. The one “so”, in the claim under In action, is Marcus’s own: 5.8 says “So you should hold dear what falls to you, for two reasons”. The reasons are that it was spun together for me out of the oldest causes, and that it is a cause of good progress for the one that governs the whole.
Says nothing about acting to change what can be changed. That is Article 2. Accepting what has happened is not an instruction to do nothing.
articles.limit: Claims 1 to 4 hold only in the first case. If you do not think the world is governed, the article reduces to claim 5, and Marcus would not object: he says so himself. That what serves the whole is good for me has one witness here (1.17); Article 6 returns to it from its own passages.

statement.t: The reason that orders the world and the reason that guides me are alike.

statement.kind: A likeness between the whole and myself
statement.form: Claims 1 and 2 describe the world and claim 3 turns to me. 5.18 says that what is supreme in me is “akin” to what is supreme in the universe; the Greek word means “of the same kind”. 4.22 argues from the order in me to order in the whole. What both give is a likeness, so the statement says “alike”, and claim 3 keeps “of one kind” on 5.18 alone. “Reason” is the word of 6.1. 5.24 says “the mind of the whole”, 6.7 “the ruling part”, and 5.18 “what is supreme” in me; the statement says “reason” for all of them, and that naming is the editor’s.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, four of the five claims gain a second author, the empty “When it breaks” gets its first item, “In action” says what worship of the governing power is enough, and “Why” gains a limit: its care may miss one person.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands and gains what follows for worship: to imitate what orders the world, by being good, is enough.

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: All this that you see, in which things divine and human are enclosed, is one
piece.follows: Everything there is, divine and human, is one.
piece.context: Seneca’s short rule for how to treat other people; “All this that you see” is the universe, things divine and human together, of which we are parts.
gives: The world is one thing

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: that divine reason too is set over all things and is itself under nothing
piece.follows: Divine reason is set over everything and answers to nothing.
piece.context: Opening of a letter that ranks the parts of a person; the rational part rules there as “that divine reason” is set over all things.
gives: What governs it is reason

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: Anyone who thinks they are unwilling to do harm is mistaken: they are not able to.
piece.follows: The gods are not merely unwilling to do harm; they are unable to.
piece.context: On the right idea of the gods, which worship needs; “they” are the gods, whom the next section says preside over the world.
gives: It has no cause to do evil

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: this reason of ours, which comes from that one, is the same
piece.follows: The reason in us is the same as the divine reason, from which it comes.
piece.context: Same opening of the letter; “this reason of ours” is the rational part of the human mind, set beside the divine reason.
gives: of one kind with it

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: the second is the one thing that is not referred to anything else but refers everything to itself
piece.follows: The rational part answers to nothing else in a person, and everything else is referred to it.
piece.context: Same opening: body serves mind and the mind’s lower parts serve its ruling part; “the second” is the rational element of that part.
gives: it turns everything else in me to its use

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: the force of all seeds, which shapes each single thing in its own way
piece.follows: Wisdom studies the force of all seeds, which shapes each thing in its own way.
piece.context: A list of what wisdom studies, as against the crafts; “it” is wisdom going back to the beginnings of things, and what shapes each thing is the force of the seeds.
gives: the power at work

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: all those things you people have listed are not many separate causes, but hang from one, from the one that makes
piece.follows: All causes depend on one cause.
piece.context: Seneca rejects Plato’s and Aristotle’s lists of causes; “all those things” are those listed causes, and the “one” is the one that makes, which he has just called reason.
gives: the one source of all things

items.label: action
items.t: To worship what governs the world, it is enough to imitate it: to be good.
items.why: Marcus says to honour what is supreme in the world. Seneca says what counts as worship enough.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Do you want to win the favour of the gods? Be good. Whoever has imitated them has worshipped them enough.
support.follows: To win the favour of the gods, be good; imitating them is worship enough.
support.context: On how the gods should be worshipped; “them” are the gods, just said to preside over the world and govern all things by their power.

items.label: breaks
items.t: It is smallness of spirit to struggle against fate and think ill of the order of the world, and to want to correct the gods sooner than myself.
items.why: Marcus has no passage in this section on what failing looks like. Seneca describes it, at the close of a letter on accepting what happens.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: the small and ignoble one, on the other hand, is the one that struggles against it and thinks ill of the order of the world and would rather correct the gods than itself
support.follows: It is a small spirit that fights fate and thinks ill of the order of the world and would sooner correct the gods than itself.
support.context: Close of a letter on accepting what happens as fate’s law; “the small and ignoble one” is the spirit that fights events instead of handing itself over to fate.

items.label: why
items.t: What governs the world guards the human race, though it is sometimes without concern for one person.
items.why: Marcus’s 7.44 speaks of a particular impulse of the world’s ruling part, and only as one of two cases; it does not say whom that impulse is for. Seneca says the gods guard humankind and may miss one person. The two do not disagree.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: who have the guardianship of the human race, sometimes without concern for individuals
support.follows: The gods guard humankind but are sometimes without concern for one person.
support.context: On what a worshipper should know of the gods; “who” refers to the gods, who preside over the world and, he adds next, neither give nor have evil.

amend.t: , and to imitate what orders the world, by being good, is worship enough

passages.title: On why advice needs underlying principles
passages.text: All this that you see, in which things divine and human are enclosed, is one; we are limbs of a great body. Nature brought us forth as kin, since she begot us from the same things and for the same things. She planted in us love for one another and made us fit for fellowship. She established what is fair and just; by her arrangement it is more wretched to harm than to be hurt; by her command let our hands be ready for those who need help.

passages.title: On reason and virtue sufficing for happiness
passages.text: I think you and I will agree that external things are acquired for the body, that the body is cared for in honour of the mind, that in the mind there are serving parts, through which we move and are nourished, given to us for the sake of the ruling part itself. In this ruling part there is something without reason, and there is also something with reason; the first serves the second, and the second is the one thing that is not referred to anything else but refers everything to itself. For that divine reason too is set over all things and is itself under nothing; and this reason of ours, which comes from that one, is the same.

passages.title: On why advice needs underlying principles
passages.text: What cause do the gods have for doing good? Nature. Anyone who thinks they are unwilling to do harm is mistaken: they are not able to. They can neither suffer a wrong nor do one, for to hurt and to be hurt are joined together. Those whom that nature, the highest and most beautiful of all, has taken out of danger it has not made dangerous either.

passages.title: On philosophy and the invention of crafts
passages.text: Then it went back to the beginnings of things, to the eternal reason set within the whole, and to the force of all seeds, which shapes each single thing in its own way. Then it began to inquire about the soul: where it comes from, where it is, how long it lasts, into how many members it is divided. Then it moved from bodies to things without body, and examined truth and its proofs thoroughly; after that, how the ambiguities of life or of speech were to be told apart; for in both, false things are mixed in with true.

passages.title: On causes and the worth of studying nature
passages.text: But what we are asking about now is the first and general cause. This must be simple, for matter too is simple. Are we asking what the cause is? Reason that makes, of course: that is, god. For all those things you people have listed are not many separate causes, but hang from one, from the one that makes.

passages.title: On why advice needs underlying principles
passages.text: The first way to worship the gods is to believe in the gods; next, to give them the majesty that is theirs, to give them the goodness without which there is no majesty; to know that it is they who preside over the world, who govern all things by their power, who have the guardianship of the human race, sometimes without concern for individuals. They neither give evil nor have it; yet they chastise some people and restrain them and impose punishments, and sometimes they punish by what looks like a good. Do you want to win the favour of the gods? Be good. Whoever has imitated them has worshipped them enough.

passages.title: On accepting fate willingly
passages.text: Let us live this way, let us speak this way; let fate find us ready and eager. This is a great spirit, the one that has handed itself over to fate; the small and ignoble one, on the other hand, is the one that struggles against it and thinks ill of the order of the world and would rather correct the gods than itself. Farewell.

claims.t: The world is one thing, ordered throughout, and all things in it are bound to one another.
claims.shared: Three passages call the world one (“one living thing”, “unity”, “the one and entire thing”), two call it ordered, and two say that all things in it are tied together. 6.8 puts order as one of two cases; 4.22 names two cases and then decides: “But in fact an order.”
claims.changed: 4.33 says more: that all things are joint causes of all the things that come about. That is kept in the practice claim. 4.22 says that all things “feel with one another”, and 4.33 speaks of a “spinning together and winding together”; the claim says “bound to one another” for both. “Throughout” is the claim’s word for what 4.22 calls “an arranged order” and sets against a jumble.

support.quote: the universe as one living thing, having one substance and one soul
support.follows: The world is one living thing with one soul.
gives: The world is one thing

support.quote: all the things that come about, exist at once within the one and entire thing, the very thing we call the universe
support.follows: All the things that happen exist at once inside one whole thing, the thing we call the universe.
gives: The world is one thing

claims.changed: 6.33 says “every kind of harm”; the claim no longer softens this to “what looks harmful”. 6.33 says “those revered and beautiful things”; the claim says “something good”. 5.24 says “mind” and does not say “governs”; the claim reads it with 6.1 as the reason that governs. 6.1 says that all things come about “in accordance with” that reason, 6.33 that they come from “that common ruling part”, and 7.44 that they follow from the impulse of “the nature of the whole”; the claim says “comes from it” for all three.

single.quote: Of the things in the universe, honour what is supreme: this is what uses all things and directs all things. In the same way, of the things in you too, honour what is supreme
single.label: An instruction
single.t: I shall honour what is supreme in the world, and in the same way what is supreme in myself.
single.why: Only 5.18 says “honour”. It is the one place where the likeness becomes an instruction.
single.follows: I should honour what is supreme in the world, and likewise what is supreme in me.

single.quote: nothing is harmed by it
single.label: A strong claim
single.t: Nothing is harmed by it.
single.why: Only 6.1 goes this far. It is kept apart so that the claim on what governs the world does not rest on it.
single.follows: Nothing is harmed by the reason that governs the world.

single.quote: or even the most important things, the ones at which the ruling part of the universe directs a particular impulse, are irrational
single.label: The second of two cases
single.t: If things did not all follow as a consequence, even the most important things, the ones the ruling part of the world aims at in particular, would be without reason.
