single.follows: If not everything follows as a consequence, then even the most important things, the ones the ruling part of the universe aims at in particular, are irrational.

single.quote: Now if it is the first, why do I even want to spend my time in a random compound and a jumble of that kind?
single.label: The other case
single.t: If the world were only confusion, why should I wish to stay in it?
single.why: Only here does Marcus say how the ungoverned case would feel. Article 3 carries his calmer answer.
single.follows: If the world were mere confusion, there would be no reason to want to remain in it.

members.text:
According to the nature of the universe all things particular are
determined, not according to any other nature, either about compassing
and containing; or within, dispersed and contained; or without,
depending. Either this universe is a mere confused mass, and an
intricate context of things, which shall in time be scattered and
dispersed again: or it is an union consisting of order, and administered
by Providence. If the first, why should I desire to continue any longer
in this fortuit confusion and commixtion? or why should I take care for
anything else, but that as soon as may be I may be earth again? And
why should I trouble myself any more whilst I seek to please the Gods?
Whatsoever I do, dispersion is my end, and will come upon me whether I
will or no. But if the latter be, then am not I religious in vain;
then will I be quiet and patient, and put my trust in Him, who is the
Governor of all.
members.english:
Each thing is carried through in accordance with the nature of the whole. For it is certainly not in accordance with any other nature, whether one that surrounds from outside, or one contained within, or one that stands apart outside.

Either a stirred brew and a mutual entanglement and a scattering, or unity and order and providence. Now if it is the first, why do I even want to spend my time in a random compound and a jumble of that kind? And why do I even care about anything other than how, one way or another, to “become earth”? And why am I even troubled? For the scattering will come upon me, whatever I do. But if it is the second, I feel reverence, I stand firm, and I take heart, relying on the one that governs.
members.greek:
Κατὰ τὴν τῶν ὅλων φύσιν ἕκαστα περαίνεται· οὐ γὰρ κατ’ ἄλλην γέ τινα φύσιν ἤτοι ἔξωθεν περιέχουσαν ἢ ἐμπεριεχομένην ἔνδον ἢ ἔξω ἀπηρτημένην.

Ἤτοι κυκεὼν καὶ ἀντεμπλοκὴ καὶ σκεδασμὸς ἢ ἕνωσις καὶ τάξις καὶ πρόνοια. εἰ μὲν οὗν τὰ πρότερα, τί καὶ ἐπιθυμῶ εἰκαίῳ συγκρίματι καὶ φυρμῷ τοιούτῳ ἐνδιατρίβειν; τί δέ μοι καὶ μέλει ἄλλου τινὸς ἢ τοῦ ὅπως ποτὲ ʽαἶα γίνεσθαιʼ; τί δὲ καὶ ταράσσομαι; ἥξει γὰρ ἐπʼ ἐμὲ ὁ σκεδασμός, ὅ τι ἂν ποιῶ. εἰ δὲ θάτερά ἐστι, σέβω καὶ εὐσταθῶ καὶ θαρρῶ τῷ διοικοῦντι.

members.text:
The nature of the universe did once certainly before it was
created, whatsoever it hath done since, deliberate and so resolve upon
the creation of the world. Now since that time, whatsoever it is, that
is and happens in the world, is either but a consequent of that one and
first deliberation: or if so be that this ruling rational part of the
world, takes any thought and care of things particular, they are surely
his reasonable and principal creatures, that are the proper object of
his particular care and providence. This often thought upon, will much
conduce to thy tranquillity.
members.english: The nature of the whole set out by impulse to make the universe. But now either everything that comes about comes about as a consequence, or even the most important things, the ones at which the ruling part of the universe directs a particular impulse, are irrational. Remembering this will make you calmer about many things.
members.greek: Ἡ τοῦ ὅλου φύσις ἐπὶ τὴν κοσμοποιίαν ὥρμησε· νῦν δὲ ἤτοι πᾶν τὸ γινόμενον κατ’ ἐπακολούθησιν γίνεται ἢ ἀλόγιστα καὶ τὰ κυριώτατά ἐστιν ἐφ’ ἃ ποιεῖται ἰδίαν ὁρμὴν τὸ τοῦ κόσμου ἡγεμονικόν. εἰς πολλά σε γαληνότερον ποιήσει τοῦτο μνημονευόμενον.

members.text:
That rational essence by which the universe is governed, is for
community and society; and therefore hath it both made the things that
are worse, for the best, and hath allied and knit together those
which are best, as it were in an harmony. Seest thou not how it hath
sub-ordinated, and co-ordinated? and how it hath distributed unto
everything according to its worth? and those which have the pre-eminency
and superiority above all, hath it united together, into a mutual
consent and agreement.
members.english: The mind of the whole is social. At any rate it has made the worse things for the sake of the better, and has fitted the better to one another. You see how it has ranked things one below another, one beside another, and has given to each according to its worth, and has brought the best things to be of one mind with one another.
members.greek: Ὁ τοῦ ὅλου νοῦς κοινωνικός. πεποίηκε γοῦν τὰ χείρω τῶν κρειττόνων ἕνεκεν καὶ τὰ κρείττω ἀλλήλοις συνήρμοσεν. ὁρᾷς πῶς ὑπέταξε, συνέταξε, καὶ τὸ κατ’ ἀξίαν ἀπένειμεν ἑκάστοις καὶ τὰ κρατιστεύοντα εἰς ὁμόνοιαν ἀλλήλων συνήγαγεν.

members.text:
The matter itself, of which the universe doth consist, is of itself
very tractable and pliable. That rational essence that doth govern it,
hath in itself no cause to do evil. It hath no evil in itself; neither
can it do anything that is evil: neither can anything be hurt by it. And
all things are done and determined according to its will and prescript.
members.english: The substance of the whole is obedient and ready, and the reason that governs it has in itself no cause for doing anything bad. For it has no badness, and it treats nothing badly, and nothing is harmed by it. And all things come about and are carried through in accordance with it.
members.greek: Ἡ τῶν ὅλων οὐσία εὐπειθὴς καὶ εὐτρεπής, ὁ δὲ ταύτην διοικῶν λόγος οὐδεμίαν ἐν ἑαυτῷ αἰτίαν ἔχει τοῦ κακοποιεῖν· κακίαν γὰρ οὐκ ἔχει οὐδέ τι κακῶς ποιεῖ οὐδὲ βλάπτεταί τι ὑπ’ ἐκείνου. πάντα δὲ κατ’ ἐκεῖνον γίνεται καὶ περαίνεται.

members.text:
Ever consider and think upon the world as being but one living
substance, and having but one soul, and how all things in the world, are
terminated into one sensitive power; and are done by one general motion
as it were, and deliberation of that one soul; and how all things that
are, concur in the cause of one another's being, and by what manner of
connection and concatenation all things happen.
members.english: To think constantly of the universe as one living thing, having one substance and one soul; and of how all things are handed up to its one perception; and how it does all things by one impulse; and how all things are joint causes of all the things that come about; and what the spinning together and winding together is like.
members.greek: Ὡς ἓν ζῷον τὸν κόσμον, μίαν οὐσίαν καὶ ψυχὴν μίαν ἐπέχον, συνεχῶς ἐπινοεῖν καὶ πῶς εἰς αἴσθησιν μίαν τὴν τούτου πάντα ἀναδίδοται καὶ πῶς ὁρμῇ μιᾷ πάντα πράσσει καὶ πῶς πάντα πάντων τῶν γινομένων συναίτια καὶ οἵα τις ἡ σύννησις καὶ συμμήρυσις.

members.text:
Consider how many different things, whether they concern our
bodies, or our souls, in a moment of time come to pass in every one of
us, and so thou wilt not wonder if many more things or rather all things
that are done, can at one time subsist, and coexist in that both one and
general, which we call the world.
members.english: Consider how many things come about at once in each of us in the same instant of time, things of the body and things of the soul together. And then you will not be surprised if many more things, or rather all the things that come about, exist at once within the one and entire thing, the very thing we call the universe.
members.greek: Ἐνθυμήθητι πόσα κατὰ τὸν αὐτὸν ἀκαριαῖον χρόνον ἐν ἑκάστῳ ἡμῶν ἅμα γίνεται σωματικὰ ὁμοῦ καὶ ψυχικά. καὶ οὕτως οὐ θαυμάσεις εἰ πολὺ πλείω, μᾶλλον δὲ πάντα τὰ γινόμενα ἐν τῷ ἑνί τε καὶ σύμπαντι, ὃ δὴ κόσμον ὀνομάζομεν, ἅμα ἐνυφίσταται.

members.text:
Either this world is a κόσμος or comely piece, because all
disposed and governed by certain order: or if it be a mixture, though
confused, yet still it is a comely piece. For is it possible that in
thee there should be any beauty at all, and that in the whole world
there should be nothing but disorder and confusion? and all things in it
too, by natural different properties one from another differenced and
distinguished; and yet all through diffused, and by natural sympathy,
one to another united, as they are?
members.english: Either an arranged order, or a stirred brew jumbled together. But in fact an order. Or can a kind of order exist in you, and disorder in the all? And this when all things are, as they are, separated out and spread out, and feel with one another.
members.greek: Ἤτοι κόσμος διατεταγμένος ἢ κυκεὼν συμπεφυρμένος. ἀλλὰ μὴν κόσμος· ἢ ἐν σοὶ μέν τις κόσμος ὑφίστασθαι δύναται, ἐν δὲ τῷ παντὶ ἀκοσμία; καὶ ταῦτα οὕτως πάντων διακεκριμένων καὶ διακεχυμένων καὶ συμπαθῶν.

members.text:
Asia, Europe; what are they, but as corners of the whole world;
of which the whole sea, is but as one drop; and the great Mount Athos,
but as a clod, as all present time is but as one point of eternity. All,
petty things; all things that are soon altered, soon perished. And all
things come from one beginning; either all severally and particularly
deliberated and resolved upon, by the general ruler and governor of all;
or all by necessary consequence. So that the dreadful hiatus of a gaping
lion, and all poison, and all hurtful things, are but (as the thorn and
the mire) the necessary consequences of goodly fair things. Think not
of these therefore, as things contrary to those which thou dost much
honour, and respect; but consider in thy mind the true fountain of all.
members.english:
Asia, Europe: corners of the universe. Every sea: a drop of the universe. Athos: a small clod of the universe. All of present time: a point of eternity. All things are small, easily changed, vanishing.

All things come from there: they have set out from that common ruling part, or they come as a consequence. So the gaping jaws of the lion too, and poison, and every kind of harm, like a thorn, like mud, are by-products of those revered and beautiful things. So do not picture them as foreign to what you revere, but consider the source of all things.
members.greek: Ἡ Ἀσία, ἡ Εὐρώπη γωνίαι τοῦ κόσμου· πᾶν πέλαγος σταγὼν τοῦ κόσμου· Ἄθως βωλάριον τοῦ κόσμου· πᾶν τὸ ἐνεστὼς τοῦ χρόνου στιγμὴ τοῦ αἰῶνος. πάντα μικρά, εὔτρεπτα, ἐναφανιζόμενα. Πάντα ἐκεῖθεν ἔρχεται, ἀπ’ ἐκείνου τοῦ κοινοῦ ἡγεμονικοῦ ὁρμήσαντα ἣ κατ’ ἐπακολούθησιν. καὶ τὸ χάσμα οὖν τοῦ λέοντος καὶ τὸ δηλητήριον καὶ πᾶσα κακουργία ὡς ἄκανθα, ὡς βόρβορος, ἐκείνων ἐπιγεννήματα τῶν σεμνῶν καὶ καλῶν. μὴ οὖν αὐτὰ ἀλλότρια τούτου οὗ σέβεις φαντάζου, ἀλλὰ τὴν πάντων πηγὴν ἐπιλογίζου.

members.text:
Honour that which is chiefest and most powerful in the world, and
that is it, which makes use of all things, and governs all things. So
also in thyself; honour that which is chiefest, and most powerful; and
is of one kind and nature with that which we now spake of. For it is the
very same, which being in thee, turneth all other things to its own use,
and by whom also thy life is governed.
members.english: Of the things in the universe, honour what is supreme: this is what uses all things and directs all things. In the same way, of the things in you too, honour what is supreme: this is what is akin to that other. For in your case too, this is what uses the others, and your life is governed by it.
members.greek: Τῶν ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ τὸ κράτιστον τίμα· ἔστι δὲ τοῦτο τὸ πᾶσι χρώμενον καὶ πάντα διέπον. ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ τῶν ἐν σοὶ τὸ κράτιστον τίμα· ἔστι δὲ τοῦτο τὸ ἐκείνῳ ὁμογενές. καὶ γὰρ ἐπὶ σοῦ τὸ τοῖς ἄλλοις χρώμενον τοῦτό ἐστι καὶ ὁ σὸς βίος ὑπὸ τούτου διοικεῖται.

members.text:
From man is the seed, that once cast into the womb man hath no
more to do with it. Another cause succeedeth, and undertakes the
work, and in time brings a child (that wonderful effect from such a
beginning!) to perfection. Again, man lets food down through his
throat; and that once down, he hath no more to do with it. Another
cause succeedeth and distributeth this food into the senses, and the
affections: into life, and into strength; and doth with it those other
many and marvellous things, that belong unto man. These things therefore
that are so secretly and invisibly wrought and brought to pass, thou
must use to behold and contemplate; and not the things themselves only,
but the power also by which they are effected; that thou mayst behold
it, though not with the eyes of the body, yet as plainly and visibly as
thou canst see and discern the outward efficient cause of the depression
and elevation of anything.
members.english: A man lets seed go into a womb and goes away, and from then on another cause takes it over, works on it and brings a baby to completion. From what a thing, what a thing! Again: he lets food go down through the throat, and from then on another cause takes it over and makes perception and impulse and, in sum, life and strength and other things (how many, and what things!). So: to look at these things that come about under such a veil, and to see the power just as we see the power that presses downward and the power that rises upward, not with the eyes, but no less clearly.
members.greek: Σπέρμα εἰς μήτραν ἀφεὶς ἀπεχώρησε καὶ λοιπὸν ἄλλη αἰτία παραλαβοῦσα ἐργάζεται καὶ ἀποτελεῖ βρέφος· ἐξ οἵου οἷον; πάλιν· τροφὴν διὰ φάρυγγος ἀφῆκε καὶ λοιπὸν ἄλλη αἰτία παραλαβοῦσα αἴσθησιν καὶ ὁρμὴν καὶ τὸ ὅλον ζωὴν καὶ ῥώμην καὶ ἄλλα (ὅσα καὶ οἷα;) ποιεῖ. ταῦτα οὖν ἐν τοιαύτῃ ἐγκαλύψει γινόμενα θεωρεῖν καὶ τὴν δύναμιν οὕτως ὁρᾶν, ὡς καὶ τὴν βρίθουσαν καὶ τὴν ἀνωφερῆ ὁρῶμεν, οὐχὶ τοῖς ὀφθαλμοῖς, ἀλλ’ οὐχ ἧττον ἐναργῶς.

members.text:
Go to the quality of the cause from which the effect doth
proceed. Behold it by itself bare and naked, separated from all that is
material. Then consider the utmost bounds of time that that cause, thus
and thus qualified, can subsist and abide.
members.english: Go to the quality of the cause; mark the cause off from the material and look at it. Then also set the limit of the time: the longest that this thing, with its own particular quality, can by nature last.
members.greek: Ἴθι ἐπὶ τὴν ποιότητα τοῦ αἰτίου καὶ ἀπὸ τοῦ ὑλικοῦ αὐτὸ περιγράψας θέασαι· εἶτα καὶ τὸν χρόνον περιόρισον, ὅσον πλεῖστον ὑφίστασθαι πέφυκε τοῦτο τὸ ἰδίως ποιόν.

members.text:
The rational commanding part, as it alone can stir up and turn
itself; so it maketh both itself to be, and everything that happeneth,
to appear unto itself, as it will itself.
members.english: The ruling part is what wakes itself and turns itself; it makes itself whatever it wants to be, and it makes everything that happens appear to itself the way it itself wants.
members.greek: Τὸ ἡγεμονικόν ἐστι τὸ ἑαυτὸ ἐγεῖρον καὶ τρέπον καὶ ποιοῦν μὲν ἑαυτὸ οἷον ἂν καὶ θέλῃ, ποιοῦν δὲ ἑαυτῷ φαίνεσθαι πᾶν τὸ συμβαῖνον οἷον αὐτὸ θέλει.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek instead of Casaubon. Passage numbers stay Casaubon’s. In modern editions 4.22 is 4.27, 4.33 is 4.40, 5.18 is 5.21, 5.24 is 5.30, 6.7 is 6.8, 6.8 is 6.9 and 6.10, 6.23 is 6.25, 6.33 is 6.36, 7.44 is 7.75 and 9.23 is 9.25; 6.1 and 10.26 are the same.
Reads four descriptions of the world as one claim, and four of what governs it as another.

Says “reason” for what Marcus names in several ways. What governs the world is “the reason that governs” in 6.1, “the mind of the whole” in 5.24 and a “ruling part” in 6.33 and 7.44. What governs me is “the ruling part” in 6.7 and “what is supreme” in me in 5.18; no passage of the section calls it reason. The second “reason” of the statement is the editor’s word.
Makes the likeness between the whole and myself the centre of the article. Only 5.18 says the two are akin; 4.22 and 6.23 argue from myself to the whole, so the statement says “alike” and no more.
Keeps “nothing is harmed by it” out of the fused claim, and keeps the second case of 7.44 apart as well.
Joins 7.44 and 6.8 on calm as a claim of its own, under “In action”.

Follows the Greek in 7.44. Casaubon has the world’s reason caring for “his reasonable and principal creatures”; the Greek says that in the second of two cases even the most important things are “irrational”. The earlier item on care for those who reason is withdrawn.

Follows the Greek where Casaubon added words. Claim 3 says “everything else in me” again, because 5.18 has “the others”, which are the other things in me. Claim 5 says “stand firm” where it said “be patient”. 10.26 no longer backs the habit in claim 4: its “thou must use to” is Casaubon’s.
articles.limit: All twelve passages are used. This is a belief about the universe and the least argued of the five. Only 5.18 says that what is supreme in me is akin to what is supreme in the world; the statement claims a likeness and no more. If you do not hold it, Articles 1 and 2 still stand on what human beings share, and Article 3 keeps its last claim.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, each claim gains a second author on one of its parts, and the article gains three things Marcus leaves out here: the answer to what I was made for, what failing at it looks like, and the joy that is left when pleasure is ruled out.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands and gains its missing step. Marcus asks what I was made for and does not answer in this section; Seneca says outright that it is reason made perfect.

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: In each thing, what ought to be best is that for which it is born, that by which it is rated.
piece.follows: In each thing, what ought to be best is what the thing is born for.
piece.context: Seneca is proving that the honourable is the only good. “What ought to be best” is each thing’s own excellence: a vine’s yield, a stag’s speed, a dog’s scent.
gives: is made for something

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: wisdom itself, which we said is both a good that belongs to others and his own
piece.follows: Wisdom is a good that belongs to others and is also the wise man’s own.
piece.context: Seneca is showing that hardship cannot stop the wise man from acting. “Wisdom itself” is what he still practises then; “his own” means the wise man’s.
gives: its fruit is shared as well as its own

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: none of the things that go out of sight and are put back into the nature of things, from which they came out and will soon come forth, is used up
piece.follows: Nothing that goes out of sight is used up: it is put back into the nature of things it came from and will soon come forth from it.
piece.context: Seneca is arguing against the fear of death. The “things” are whatever dies or disappears, which he says will return; he is not speaking of waste or flaws.
gives: she takes it back into herself

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: Let us embrace it and love it; it is full of pleasure, if you know how to use it. Fruit is most welcome when it is slipping away
piece.follows: Old age is full of pleasure for one who knows how to use it, as fruit is most welcome when it is slipping away.
piece.context: Seneca has just scolded his decaying house, his gnarled trees and an old slave, and seen his own age in them. “It” is old age; the fruit is his comparison.
gives: it has something pleasing of its own

items.label: why
items.t: What is peculiar to me as a human being is reason. Reason made perfect is what I am born for, and when I fulfil it my good is brought to completion.
items.why: Marcus asks in 8.17 what I am for, and whether it is pleasure, but this section never gives the answer. Seneca gives it in so many words.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: What is peculiar to a human being? Reason
support.follows: What belongs to a human being alone is reason.
support.context: The same proof that the honourable is the only good. “Peculiar to a human being” means what a human being has and animals and plants do not.
gives: What is peculiar to me as a human being is reason

support.author: seneca
support.quote: The mind, and reason made perfect in the mind.
support.follows: What is a person’s own is the mind, and reason made perfect in it.
support.context: Seneca is saying what to praise in a person: not his slaves, house or income, which are outside him. The words answer the question of what is “man’s own”, the thing peculiar to a human being.
gives: Reason made perfect

support.author: seneca
support.quote: his good is brought to completion if he has fulfilled what he is born for
support.follows: A person’s good is brought to completion when he fulfils what he is born for.
support.context: The close of the same argument. “What he is born for” is the reason just named, made perfect in the mind.
gives: what I am born for
when I fulfil it my good is brought to completion

items.label: action
items.t: I am not to go without gladness. True joy is a stern thing, and I take my joy from what is my own.
items.why: Marcus asks whether I am for pleasure and expects a no (8.17). He does not say in this section what joy is left; 9.8 says only that reason has fruit of its own. Seneca says what joy remains and where it comes from.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: I do not want gladness ever to be lacking to you
support.follows: Seneca does not want his friend ever to be without gladness.
support.context: Seneca tells Lucilius to learn how to feel joy and denies he is taking pleasures from him. “Gladness” is the kind born inside a person, not a gift of chance.
gives: I am not to go without gladness

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Believe me, true joy is a stern thing.
support.follows: True joy is serious, not light.
support.context: “True joy” is that of a person who can despise death, face poverty and curb his pleasures. Seneca sets it against laughter and a cheerful face.
gives: True joy is a stern thing

support.author: seneca
support.quote: take your joy from what is your own
support.follows: I should take my joy from what is within myself.
support.context: Said after telling Lucilius to trample what shines on the outside. “What is your own” is, in his next words, yourself and the best part of you.
gives: I take my joy from what is my own

items.label: breaks
items.t: I am alive when I am of use to many and make use of myself. If I lie hidden and inert, I have gone ahead of my own death; and if I go into hiding out of fear, I live not for myself but for my belly, for sleep and for lust.
items.why: Marcus has no passage in this section on what failing looks like. Seneca describes it twice: the man who is of use to no one, and the man who hides out of fear.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: The one who is of use to many is alive; the one who makes use of himself is alive.
support.follows: To be alive is to be of use to many and to make use of oneself.
support.context: The letter attacks living for the belly. “The one” is set against those who obey their appetites, some of whom Seneca has just counted among the dead.
gives: I am alive when I am of use to many and make use of myself

support.author: seneca
support.quote: those who lie hidden and inert are in their house as they would be in a tomb
support.follows: People who lie hidden and inert are in their house as if in a tomb.
support.context: “Those who lie hidden” are the opposite of the man of use to many: people who withdraw into sloth, in a letter about living for the belly.
gives: If I lie hidden and inert

support.author: seneca
support.quote: they have gone ahead of their own death
support.follows: Such people have gone ahead of their own death.
support.context: “They” are the same inert people. Seneca says their name may be carved on marble at the very threshold of the house, as on a tomb.
gives: I have gone ahead of my own death

support.author: seneca
support.quote: who has gone into hiding out of fear
support.follows: The man in question has gone into hiding out of fear.
support.context: Seneca is at the villa of Vatia, who was famous only for his leisure, and separates leisure from hiding. “Who” is the man who has run away from affairs and from people.
gives: if I go into hiding out of fear

support.author: seneca
support.quote: that man does not live for himself but, which is the most shameful thing, for his belly, for sleep, for lust
support.follows: A man who hides like that does not live for himself; he lives for his belly, for sleep and for lust.
support.context: “That man” is the man who has hidden from affairs and people out of fear and failed desires. It is not anyone at rest, nor anyone enjoying himself.
gives: I live not for myself but for my belly, for sleep and for lust

passages.title: On learning in old age and the only good
passages.text: Every thing rests on its own good. What recommends the vine is its fruitfulness and the flavour of its wine; what recommends the stag is speed. Of pack animals, whose one use is this, to carry a load, you ask how strong they are in the back. In a dog the first thing is keenness of scent if it has to track wild animals, running if it has to catch them, boldness if it has to bite and attack. In each thing, what ought to be best is that for which it is born, that by which it is rated.

passages.title: On rejecting even moderate passions
passages.text: The wise man is not harmed by poverty, nor by pain, nor by the other storms of life. For not all his work is prevented, but only the work that is for others: he himself is always in action, greatest in what he achieves at the time when fortune has set itself against him; for then he is doing the business of wisdom itself, which we said is both a good that belongs to others and his own.

passages.title: On the benefits of a quiet life
passages.text: But if so great a desire for a longer life has hold of you, consider that none of the things that go out of sight and are put back into the nature of things, from which they came out and will soon come forth, is used up: these things stop, they do not perish, and death, which we dread and refuse, interrupts life, it does not snatch it away; a day will come again to put us back into the light, a day that many would refuse if it did not bring them back with their memory gone.

passages.title: On old age and living each day fully
passages.text: I owe this to my country place near the city: my old age showed itself to me wherever I turned. Let us embrace it and love it; it is full of pleasure, if you know how to use it. Fruit is most welcome when it is slipping away; the beauty of boyhood is greatest at its close; those given over to wine are delighted by the last drink, the one that sinks them, the one that puts the finishing touch to drunkenness;

passages.title: On learning in old age and the only good
passages.text: What is peculiar to a human being? Reason: when this is right and brought to its full measure, it has made a human being’s happiness complete. So if every thing, when it has perfected its own good, is praiseworthy and has reached the goal of its nature, and if a human being’s own good is reason, then if he has perfected this he is praiseworthy and has touched the goal of his nature. This perfected reason is called virtue, and it is also what is honourable.

passages.title: On the god within us
passages.text: Praise in him what can neither be snatched away nor given, what is man’s own. You ask what that is? The mind, and reason made perfect in the mind. For man is a reasoning animal; and so his good is brought to completion if he has fulfilled what he is born for.

passages.title: On finding true joy within
passages.text: Do this before all else, my Lucilius: learn to feel joy. Do you now think that I am taking many pleasures away from you, I who clear away the things of chance, who think that hopes, the sweetest of delights, are to be avoided? No, on the contrary: I do not want gladness ever to be lacking to you. I want it to be born for you at home: it is born if only it comes about within yourself. The other kinds of cheerfulness do not fill the breast; they smooth the brow, they are slight, unless perhaps you judge that a man who laughs is feeling joy: the mind ought to be lively and confident and raised up above all things.

passages.title: On finding true joy within
passages.text: Believe me, true joy is a stern thing. Or do you think that anyone with a relaxed and, as those pampered people say, “cheery little” face despises death, opens his house to poverty, holds pleasures under the bridle, rehearses the endurance of pains? The man who turns these things over within himself is in great joy, but a joy with little charm. It is this joy that I want you to be in possession of: it will never fail, once you have found where it is to be got from.

passages.title: On finding true joy within
passages.text: Do, I beg you, dearest Lucilius, the one thing that can make a person happy: scatter and trample those things that shine on the outside, that are promised to you by someone else or from something else; look to the true good and take your joy from what is your own. But what is this “from what is your own”? From yourself, and from the best part of you. As for the little body too, even though nothing can be done without it, believe it to be a necessary thing rather than a great one; it supplies empty pleasures, short ones, ones to be regretted and, unless they are tempered with great moderation, bound to pass into their opposite. This is what I say: pleasure is on a steep slope; it tilts towards pain unless it has kept within bounds; but to keep within bounds is difficult in a thing that you have believed to be good: greed for the true good is safe.

passages.title: On harmful prayers and human greed
passages.text: So let us count these people, who are, as Sallust says, “obedient to the belly”, as animals, not as human beings, and some of them not even as animals, but as the dead. The one who is of use to many is alive; the one who makes use of himself is alive. But those who lie hidden and inert are in their house as they would be in a tomb. You may carve their name on marble at the very threshold: they have gone ahead of their own death. Farewell.

passages.title: On hiding versus truly living in retirement
passages.text: For the man who has run away from affairs and from people, whom the ill success of his own desires has banished, who could not bear to see others more successful, who has gone into hiding out of fear like a timid and sluggish animal: that man does not live for himself but, which is the most shameful thing, for his belly, for sleep, for lust; a man who lives for no one does not, just by that, live for himself. Yet steadiness, and persistence in one’s purpose, is so great a thing that even stubborn sluggishness carries weight.

claims.t: Everything that exists, the gods included, is made for something and bears fruit in its own time.
claims.shared: Both passages name the gods: 8.17 has the Sun and “the other gods”, 9.8 has “god”. What they say of them differs: 8.17 says each thing has come to be for something, 9.8 says a human being, god and the universe bear fruit, each in its own seasons.
claims.changed: “Made for something” and “bears fruit” are kept as two phrases, each from its own passage. “Made for” is the claim’s plain English for 8.17’s “has come to be for”; the Greek names no maker. “Everything that exists” is 8.17’s “each thing”. 9.8 names only a human being, god and the universe; when the claim says that everything bears fruit, it widens 9.8. Drops the horse, the vine and the Sun as examples.

support.quote: Each thing has come to be for something: a horse, a vine.
support.follows: Each thing has come to be for something, as a horse or a vine has.
gives: Everything that exists
is made for something

support.quote: Even the Sun will say, “I have come to be for some work,” and so will the other gods.
support.follows: Even the Sun would say it has come to be for some work, and the other gods would say the same.

is made for something

support.quote: A human being bears fruit, and so does god, and so does the universe
support.follows: A human being, god and the universe each bear fruit.

claims.t: I was not made to please myself, but to keep exercising reason and fellowship. Reason turns toward other people, and its fruit is shared as well as its own.
claims.shared: Two passages say that reason is not a private thing, in different words: 6.13 honours rational soul “as civic” and keeps the soul “rational and social”; 9.8 says reason has fruit “both shared and its own”. “Social” and “shared” translate Greek words of one family. “Turns toward other people” is the claim’s phrase for both; neither passage uses it. The rest is one passage each: 8.17 asks whether I am for pleasure, 6.13 names the keeping of the soul, 9.8 the fruit.
claims.changed: 8.17 asks what I am for, offers pleasure as an answer and says “See whether the idea holds up.” It expects a no and does not say it; the claim says it. The “but” that answers the question is the editor’s, and is marked.

inferences.why: 8.17 asks what I am for and challenges only pleasure as an answer. The answer is the editor’s, taken from 6.13 and 9.8, which do not say what I have come to be for.

support.quote: So what are you for? For pleasure?
support.follows: I should ask what I am for, and whether it can be pleasure.
gives: not made to please myself
support.note: The question is put to the reader. Its verb is understood from the Sun’s words just before it: what have you come to be for?

support.quote: See whether the idea holds up.
support.follows: I should test whether that idea holds up; Marcus expects that it will not, and leaves the verdict to me.
gives: not made to please myself

support.quote: before everything else preserves their own soul rational and social in its condition and its movement
support.follows: Such a person, before everything else, keeps their own soul rational and social, in its state and in what it does.
gives: to keep exercising reason and fellowship

support.quote: whoever honours rational soul as such, and as civic
support.follows: This person honours rational soul as such, and as civic: as something that belongs to a community.
gives: Reason turns toward other people

support.quote: from it come other things of much the same kind as reason itself
support.follows: What comes from reason is of much the same kind as reason itself.
gives: its fruit

support.quote: reason has fruit, both shared and its own
support.follows: Reason has fruit that is shared and fruit that is its own.
gives: Reason turns toward other people
its fruit is shared as well as its own

claims.t: What looks rotten or old to me looks different to someone who knows nature well. Nature throws nothing away: she takes it back into herself and makes new things out of it, and it has something pleasing of its own.
claims.shared: Both passages speak of the rotten and the old, and both appeal to a person who knows nature, who sees them differently: in 8.48 “a person who studies nature” laughs at the complaint, in 3.2 only “the one who has become truly at home with nature and its works” is struck by the beauty. What that person sees differs: 8.48 says nature reuses such things, 3.2 says they are pleasing as they are.
claims.changed: Does not make “by-products” the common term. They are the subject of 3.2 from its first sentence (“what comes about on top of the things that come about by nature”), but 8.48 has shavings and trimmings only as a comparison. The claim rests on the two things both passages say outright. The claim calls nature “she”; the translation says “it”.

support.quote: changes into itself everything inside that seems to be decaying and growing old and to be useless, and that it makes other, fresh things again out of these very things
support.follows: What seems spoiled, old or useless, nature changes into herself and makes into new things.

support.quote: they, at least, have somewhere to throw these, whereas the nature of the whole has nothing outside it

support.quote: in olives ripened on the tree, the very nearness to rotting adds a certain beauty of its own to the fruit

support.quote: there is almost nothing, even among the things that happen as consequences, that will not seem to that person to be put together in a way that somehow gives pleasure

single.quote: A bitter cucumber? Leave it. Brambles in the path? Turn aside. That is enough.
single.label: A practice
single.t: If the cucumber is bitter, I set it aside; if brambles are in the way, I go round them. That is enough.
single.why: Only 8.48 gives the practice. Its second half is the next item.
single.follows: I should set the bitter thing aside, go round the obstacle, and leave it at that.

single.quote: Do not go on to say, “And why did these things come to be in the universe at all?”
single.label: A prohibition
single.t: I do not go on to ask why a bitter thing came to be in the universe at all.
single.why: Only 8.48 forbids the question. Its reason is under “If I doubt it”: nature throws nothing away. Marcus does not say how this fits with 8.17, where each thing has come to be for something.
single.follows: I should not go on to ask why such things came to be in the universe at all.

single.quote: what is done impulse by impulse; and in the latter case see at once what aim it is directed at
single.label: A practice
single.t: I follow what is done impulse by impulse, and I see at once what aim each one is directed at.
single.why: Only 7.4 asks about the aim of what is done, impulse by impulse. It speaks of what is said and done, not of what each thing has come to be for, so it backs no claim.
single.follows: I should follow what is done impulse by impulse and see at once what aim it is directed at.

members.text:
This also thou must observe, that whatsoever it is that naturally
doth happen to things natural, hath somewhat in itself that is pleasing
and delightful: as a great loaf when it is baked, some parts of it
cleave as it were, and part asunder, and make the crust of it rugged and
unequal, and yet those parts of it, though in some sort it be against
the art and intention of baking itself, that they are thus cleft and
parted, which should have been and were first made all even and uniform,
they become it well nevertheless, and have a certain peculiar property,
to stir the appetite. So figs are accounted fairest and ripest then,
when they begin to shrink, and wither as it were. So ripe olives, when
they are next to putrefaction, then are they in their proper beauty. The
hanging down of grapes--the brow of a lion, the froth of a foaming wild
boar, and many other like things, though by themselves considered, they
are far from any beauty, yet because they happen naturally, they both
are comely, and delightful; so that if a man shall with a profound mind
and apprehension, consider all things in the world, even among all those
things which are but mere accessories and natural appendices as it were,
there will scarce appear anything unto him, wherein he will not find
matter of pleasure and delight. So will he behold with as much pleasure
the true _rictus_ of wild beasts, as those which by skilful painters and
other artificers are imitated. So will he be able to perceive the proper
ripeness and beauty of old age, whether in man or woman: and whatsoever
else it is that is beautiful and alluring in whatsoever is, with chaste
and continent eyes he will soon find out and discern. Those and many
other things will he discern, not credible unto every one, but unto them
only who are truly and familiarly acquainted, both with nature itself,
and all natural things.
members.english: One should also take note of things like this: that even what comes about on top of the things that come about by nature has something graceful and attractive about it. For example, when bread is baking, some parts of it break open at the side; and so these parts too, which stand open like this and are in a way contrary to what the baker’s craft sets out to do, somehow look right and stir up an eagerness for the food in a way of their own. Again, figs gape open when they are at their ripest; and in olives ripened on the tree, the very nearness to rotting adds a certain beauty of its own to the fruit. And ears of grain bending down, and the frown on the lion’s brow, and the foam running from the mouths of wild boars, and many other things are far from good-looking if one looks at them by themselves; and yet, because they come as consequences of the things that come about by nature, they help to adorn them and they charm the mind. So if someone has a deeper feeling for, and understanding of, the things that come about in the whole, there is almost nothing, even among the things that happen as consequences, that will not seem to that person to be put together in a way that somehow gives pleasure. And that person will look even at the real gaping jaws of wild animals with no less pleasure than at all those that painters and sculptors show in imitation; and will be able to see a kind of prime and ripeness in an old woman and an old man, and to see with their own chaste eyes the seductive charm of the young. And many such things, which will not convince everyone, will strike only the one who has become truly at home with nature and its works.
members.greek: Χρὴ καὶ τὰ τοιαῦτα παραφυλάσσειν, ὅτι καὶ τὰ ἐπιγινόμενα τοῖς φύσει γινομένοις ἔχει τι εὔχαρι καὶ ἐπαγωγόν. οἷον ἄρτου ὀπτωμένου παραρρήγνυταί τινα μέρη· καὶ ταῦτα οὖν τὰ διέχοντα οὕτως καὶ τρόπον τινὰ παρὰ τὸ ἐπάγγελμα τῆς ἀρτοποιίας ἔχοντα ἐπιπρέπει πως καὶ προθυμίαν πρὸς τὴν τροφὴν ἰδίως ἀνακινεῖ. πάλιν τε τὰ σῦκα ὁπότε ὡραιότατά ἐστι, κέχηνε καὶ ἐν ταῖς δρυπεπέσιν ἐλαίαις αὐτὸ τὸ ἐγγὺς τῇ σήψει ἴδιόν τι κάλλος τῷ καρπῷ προστίθησι. καὶ οἱ στάχυες κάτω νεύοντες καὶ τὸ τοῦ λέοντος ἐπισκύνιον καὶ ὁ τῶν συῶν ἐκ τοῦ στόματος ῥέων ἀφρὸς καὶ πολλὰ ἕτερα, κατ’ ἰδίαν εἴ τις σκοποίη, πόρρω ὄντα τοῦ εὐειδοῦς, ὅμως διὰ τὸ τοῖς φύσει γινομένοις ἐπακολουθεῖν συνεπικοσμεῖ καὶ ψυχαγωγεῖ· ὥστε, εἴ τις ἔχει πάθος καὶ ἔννοιαν βαθυτέραν πρὸς τὰ ἐν τῷ ὅλῳ γινόμενα, σχεδὸν οὐδὲν οὐχὶ δόξει αὐτῷ καὶ τῶν κατ’ ἐπακολούθησιν συμβαινόντων ἡδέως πως διασυνίστασθαι. οὗτος δὲ καὶ θηρίων ἀληθῆ χάσματα οὐχ ἧσσον ἡδέως ὄψεται ἢ ὅσα γραφεῖς καὶ πλάσται μιμούμενοι δεικνύουσιν, καὶ γραὸς καὶ γέροντος ἀκμήν τινα καὶ ὥραν καὶ τὸ ἐν παισὶν ἐπαφρόδιτον τοῖς ἑαυτοῦ σώφροσιν ὀφθαλμοῖς ὁρᾶν δυνήσεται· καὶ πολλὰ τοιαῦτα οὐ παντὶ πιθανά, μόνῳ δὲ τῷ πρὸς τὴν φύσιν καὶ τὰ ταύτης ἔργα γνησίως ᾠκειωμένῳ προσπεσεῖται.

members.text:
Those things which the common sort of people do admire, are most
of them such things as are very general, and may be comprehended under
things merely natural, or naturally affected and qualified: as stones,
wood, figs, vines, olives. Those that be admired by them that are more
moderate and restrained, are comprehended under things animated: as
flocks and herds. Those that are yet more gentle and curious, their
admiration is commonly confined to reasonable creatures only; not in
general as they are reasonable, but as they are capable of art, or of
some craft and subtile invention: or perchance barely to reasonable
creatures; as they that delight in the possession of many slaves. But
he that honours a reasonable soul in general, as it is reasonable and
naturally sociable, doth little regard anything else: and above all
things is careful to preserve his own, in the continual habit and
exercise both of reason and sociableness: and thereby doth co-operate
with him, of whose nature he doth also participate; God.
members.english: Most of the things the crowd admires come down to the most general kind, the things held together by cohesion or by natural growth: stones, timber, fig trees, vines, olive trees. The things admired by people of a slightly better sort come down to the things held together by soul, such as flocks and herds. The things admired by people more refined still come down to the things held together by rational soul; not, however, rational soul as such, but in so far as it is skilled in a craft or adept in some other way, or merely in terms of owning a great number of slaves. But whoever honours rational soul as such, and as civic, no longer pays attention to any of the other things, but before everything else preserves their own soul rational and social in its condition and its movement, and works together with whoever is of the same kind toward this.
members.greek: Τὰ πλεῖστα, ὦν ἡ πληθὺς θαυμάζει, εἰς γενικώτατα ἀνάγεται τὰ ὑπὸ ἕξεως ἣ φύσεως συνεχόμενα, λίθους, ξύλα, συκᾶς, ἀμπέλους, ἐλαίας· τὰ δὲ ὑπὸ τῶν ὀλίγῳ μετριωτέρων εἰς τὰ ὑπὸ ψυχῆς, οἶον ποίμνας, ἀγέλας· τὰ δὲ ὑπὸ τῶν ἔτι χαριεστέρων εἰς τὰ ὑπὸ λογικῆς ψυχῆς, οὐ μέντοι καθολικῆς, ἀλλὰ καθὸ τεχνικὴ ἢ ἄλλως πως ἐντρεχής, ἢ κατὰ ψιλὸν τὸ πλῆθος ἀνδραπόδων κεκτῆσθαι. ὁ δὲ ψυχὴν λογικὴν καθολικὴν καὶ πολιτικὴν τιμῶν οὐδὲν ἔτι τῶν ἄλλων ἐπιστρέφεται, πρὸ ἁπάντων δὲ τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ψυχὴν λογικῶς καὶ κοινωνικῶς ἔχουσαν καὶ κινουμένην διασῴζει καὶ τῷ ὁμογενεῖ εἰς τοῦτο συνεργεῖ.

members.text:
Whatsoever is, was made for something: as a horse, a vine. Why
wonderest thou? The sun itself will say of itself, I was made for
something; and so hath every god its proper function. What then were
then made for? to disport and delight thyself? See how even common sense
and reason cannot brook it.
members.english: Each thing has come to be for something: a horse, a vine. Why are you surprised? Even the Sun will say, “I have come to be for some work,” and so will the other gods. So what are you for? For pleasure? See whether the idea holds up.
members.greek: Ἕκαστον πρός τι γέγονεν, ἵππος, ἄμπελος. τί θαυμάζεις; καὶ ὁ Ἥλιος ἐρεῖ· πρός τι ἔργου γέγονα, καὶ οἱ λοιποὶ θεοί. σὺ οὖν πρὸς τί; τὸ ἥδεσθαι; ἴδε εἰ ἀνέχεται ἡ ἔννοια.

members.text:
Is the cucumber bitter? set it away. Brambles are in the way?
avoid them. Let this suffice. Add not presently speaking unto thyself,
What serve these things for in the world? For, this, one that is
acquainted with the mysteries of nature, will laugh at thee for it; as a
carpenter would or a shoemaker, if meeting in either of their shops with
some shavings, or small remnants of their work, thou shouldest blame
them for it. And yet those men, it is not for want of a place where to
throw them that they keep them in their shops for a while: but the
nature of the universe hath no such out-place; but herein doth consist
the wonder of her art and skill, that she having once circumscribed
herself within some certain bounds and limits, whatsoever is within her
that seems either corrupted, or old, or unprofitable, she can change it
into herself, and of these very things can make new things; so that she
needeth not to seek elsewhere out of herself either for a new supply of
matter and substance, or for a place where to throw out whatsoever is
irrecoverably putrid and corrupt. Thus she, as for place, so for matter
and art, is herself sufficient unto herself.
members.english: A bitter cucumber? Leave it. Brambles in the path? Turn aside. That is enough. Do not go on to say, “And why did these things come to be in the universe at all?” Because you will be laughed at by a person who studies nature, just as you would be laughed at by a carpenter and a shoemaker if you blamed them because you see, in the workshop, shavings and trimmings from the things being made. And yet they, at least, have somewhere to throw these, whereas the nature of the whole has nothing outside it. But the wonderful thing about this craft is that nature, having drawn a boundary around itself, changes into itself everything inside that seems to be decaying and growing old and to be useless, and that it makes other, fresh things again out of these very things, so that it neither needs substance from outside nor has any further need of a place to throw out what is too rotten. So its own space is enough for it, and its own material, and its own craft.
members.greek: Σίκυος πικρός; ἄφες. βάτοι ἐν τῇ ὁδῷ; ἔκκλινον. ἀρκεῖ, μὴ προσεπείπῃς· τί δὲ καὶ ἐγένετο ταῦτα ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ; ἐπεὶ καταγελασθήσῃ ὑπὸ ἀνθρώπου φυσιολόγου, ὡς ἂν καὶ ὑπὸ τέκτονος καὶ σκυτέως γελασθείης καταγινώσκων ὅτι ἐν τῷ ἐργαστηρίῳ ξέσματα καὶ περιτμήματα τῶν κατασκευαζομένων ὁρᾷς. καίτοι ἐκεῖνοί γε ἔχουσι ποῦ αὐτὰ ῥίψωσιν, ἡ δὲ τῶν ὅλων φύσις ἔξω οὐδὲν ἔχει, ἀλλὰ τὸ θαυμαστὸν τῆς τέχνης ταύτης ἐστὶν ὅτι περιορίσασα ἑαυτὴν πᾶν τὸ ἔνδον διαφθείρεσθαι καὶ γηράσκειν καὶ ἄχρηστον εἶναι δοκοῦν εἰς ἑαυτὴν μεταβάλλει, καὶ ὅτι πάλιν ἄλλα νεαρὰ ἐκ τούτων αὐτῶν ποιεῖ, ἵνα μήτε οὐσίας ἔξωθεν χρῄζῃ μήτε ὅπου ἐκβάλῃ τὰ σαπρότερα προσδέηται. ἀρκεῖται οὖν καὶ χώρᾳ τῇ ἑαυτῆς καὶ ὕλῃ τῇ ἑαυτῆς καὶ τέχνῃ τῇ ἰδίᾳ.

members.text:
Man, God, the world, every one in their kind, bear some fruits.
All things have their proper time to bear. Though by custom, the word
itself is in a manner become proper unto the vine, and the like, yet is
it so nevertheless, as we have said. As for reason, that beareth both
common fruit for the use of others; and peculiar, which itself doth
enjoy. Reason is of a diffusive nature, what itself is in itself, it
begets in others, and so doth multiply.
members.english: A human being bears fruit, and so does god, and so does the universe; each bears it in its own seasons. But if usage has made the phrase well worn, in its strict sense, for the vine and things like it, that makes no difference. And reason has fruit, both shared and its own, and from it come other things of much the same kind as reason itself.
members.greek: Φέρει καρπὸν καὶ ἄνθρωπος καὶ θεὸς καὶ ὁ κόσμος· ἐν ταῖς οἰκείαις ὥραις ἕκαστα φέρει. εἰ δὲ ἡ συνήθεια κυρίως τέτριφεν ἐπὶ ἀμπέλου καὶ τῶν ὁμοίων, οὐδὲν τοῦτο. ὁ λόγος δὲ καὶ κοινὸν καὶ ἴδιον καρπὸν ἔχει καὶ γίνεται ἐξ αὐτοῦ τοιαῦθ’ ἕτερα, ὁποῖόν τι αὐτός ἐστιν ὁ λόγος.

members.text:
Word after word, every one by itself, must the things that are
spoken be conceived and understood; and so the things that are done,
purpose after purpose, every one by itself likewise. And as in matter of
purposes and actions, we must presently see what is the proper use and
relation of every one; so of words must we be as ready, to consider of
every one what is the true meaning, and signification of it according to
truth and nature, however it be taken in common use.
members.english: One must follow what is said word by word, and what is done impulse by impulse; and in the latter case see at once what aim it is directed at, and in the former watch closely for what is meant.
members.greek: Δεῖ κατὰ λέξιν παρακολουθεῖν τοῖς λεγομένοις καὶ καθ’ ἑκάστην ὁρμὴν τοῖς γινομένοις, καὶ ἐπὶ μὲν τοῦ ἑτέρου εὐθὺς ὁρᾶν ἐπὶ τίνα σκοπὸν ἡ ἀναφορά, ἐπὶ δὲ τοῦ ἑτέρου παραφυλάσσειν τί τὸ σημαινόμενον.

members.why: What tragedy and comedy were brought on for. Purpose applied to drama, with nothing for a rule of life.
members.text:
Tragedies were at first brought in and instituted, to put men in mind
of worldly chances and casualties: that these things in the ordinary
course of nature did so happen: that men that were much pleased and
delighted by such accidents upon this stage, would not by the same
things in a greater stage be grieved and afflicted: for here you see
what is the end of all such things; and that even they that cry out
so mournfully to Cithaeron, must bear them for all their cries and
exclamations, as well as others. And in very truth many good things are
spoken by these poets; as that (for example) is an excellent passage:
'But if so be that I and my two children be neglected by the Gods, they
have some reason even for that,' &c. And again, 'It will but little
avail thee to storm and rage against the things themselves,' &c. Again,
'To reap one's life, as a ripe ear of corn;' and whatsoever else is
to be found in them, that is of the same kind. After the tragedy, the
ancient comedy was brought in, which had the liberty to inveigh against
personal vices; being therefore through this her freedom and liberty
of speech of very good use and effect, to restrain men from pride
and arrogancy. To which end it was, that Diogenes took also the same
liberty. After these, what were either the Middle, or New Comedy
admitted for, but merely, (Or for the most part at least) for the
delight and pleasure of curious and excellent imitation? 'It will steal
away; look to it,' &c. Why, no man denies, but that these also have some
good things whereof that may be one: but the whole drift and foundation
of that kind of dramatical poetry, what is it else, but as we have said?
members.english: First, tragedies were brought on as reminders of the things that happen, and that it is in the nature of these things to happen this way, and that what charms you on the stage should not weigh on you on the larger stage. For you see that these things have to be carried through this way, and that even those who cry out “O Cithaeron!” bear them. And some things are said usefully by those who write the plays. This above all, for example: “But if I and my two children have been neglected by the gods, this too has its reason.” And again: “For one should not be angry with events.” And: “To reap life like a fruitful ear of grain.” And everything of that kind. After tragedy, the Old Comedy was brought on. It had a tutor’s frankness and, by its very plainness of speech, reminded people, not uselessly, of freedom from conceit. It was for some such purpose that Diogenes too took these things up. As for the Middle Comedy after it, and lastly the New, which little by little slipped down into cleverness at imitation, consider just what it has been taken up for. For it is not unknown that some useful things are said by these writers too; but the whole undertaking of this kind of poetry and play-making, just what aim did it look to?
members.greek: Πρῶτον αἱ τραγῳδίαι παρήχθησαν ὑπομνηστικαὶ τῶν συμβαινόντων καὶ ὅτι ταῦτα οὕτως πέφυκε γίνεσθαι καὶ ὅτι, οἷς ἐπὶ τῆς σκηνῆς ψυχαγωγεῖσθε, τούτοις μὴ ἄχθεσθε ἐπὶ τῆς μείζονος σκηνῆς· ὁρᾶτε γὰρ ὅτι οὕτως δεῖ ταῦτα περαίνεσθαι καὶ ὅτι φέρουσιν αὐτὰ καὶ οἱ κεκραγότες· ʽἰὼ Κιθαιρών.ʼ καὶ λέγεται δέ τινα ὑπὸ τῶν τὰ δράματα ποιούντων χρησίμως· οἷόν ἐστιν ἐκεῖνο μάλιστα· εἰ δ’ ἠμελήθην ἐκ θεῶν καὶ παῖδ’ ἐμώ, ἔχει λόγον καὶ τοῦτο· καὶ πάλιν· τοῖς πράγμασιν γὰρ οὐχὶ θυμοῦσθαι· καί· βίον θερίζειν ὥστε κάρπιμον στάχυν· καὶ ὅσα τοιαῦτα. μετὰ δὲ τὴν τραγῳδίαν ἡ ἀρχαία κωμῳδία παρήχθη, παιδαγωγικὴν παρρησίαν ἔχουσα καὶ τῆς ἀτυφίας οὐκ ἀχρήστως δι’ αὐτῆς τῆς εὐθυρρημοσύνης ὑπομιμνῄσκουσα· πρὸς οἷόν τι καὶ Διογένης ταυτὶ παρελάμβανε. μετὰ ταύτην ἡ μέση κωμῳδία καὶ λοιπὸν ἡ νέα πρὸς τί ποτε παρείληπται, ἣ κατ’ ὀλίγον ἐπὶ τὴν ἐκ μιμήσεως φιλοτεχνίαν ὑπερρύη, ἐπίστησον. ὅτι μὲν γὰρ λέγεται καὶ ὑπὸ τούτων τινὰ χρήσιμα οὐκ ἀγνοεῖται, ἀλλὰ ἡ ὅλη ἐπιβολὴ τῆς τοιαύτης ποιήσεως καὶ δραματουργίας πρὸς τίνα ποτὲ σκοπὸν ἀπέβλεψεν;

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek instead of Casaubon. Passage numbers stay Casaubon’s. In modern editions 6.13 is 6.14, 8.17 is 8.19, 8.48 is 8.50, 9.8 is 9.10 and 11.5 is 11.6; 3.2 and 7.4 are the same.
Uses 6.13 and 9.8 to answer the question that 8.17 asks and leaves open. The step is marked as the editor’s: “namely” in the statement, “but” in claim 2.

Fuses 8.17 with 9.8 only on what both say: the gods are included. “Made for something” is 8.17’s and “bears fruit” is 9.8’s, and the claim keeps them apart. “Everything that exists” is 8.17’s “each thing”; 9.8 names a human being, god and the universe.
Fuses 6.13 with 9.8 on reason turning toward other people. The phrase is the editor’s for 6.13’s “civic” and “social” and for 9.8’s fruit “both shared and its own”.
Fuses 8.48 with 3.2, the most central passage of the section, on the rotten and the old and on the person who knows nature. That nature reuses them is 8.48 alone; that they are pleasing is 3.2 alone.
Keeps 7.4 as a said-once practice. It was a witness to claim 1 without backing any of its words.

8.17 says each thing has come to be for something; 8.48 forbids asking why a bitter thing came to be at all. The translation has “come to be” in both because the Greek has one verb in both. Neither passage mentions the other, and the article keeps both without reconciling them.

Withdraws “by nature” from the statement and from claim 2, and “of its own kind” from claim 1. They rested on words Casaubon added: “naturally sociable” in 6.13, where the Greek has “civic”; “of a diffusive nature” and “every one in their kind” in 9.8, where the Greek has nothing.
Keeps “made for” in the title, the statement and the claims as plain English for 8.17’s “has come to be for”. The Greek names no maker.

Keeps “I was not made to please myself”, although 8.17 only asks “For pleasure?” and says “See whether the idea holds up.” Casaubon turned that into a verdict; the Greek leaves the verdict to the reader.
articles.limit: This is the smallest and loosest section: seven passages, six used. Claims 1 and 3 rest on two passages and claim 2 on three, and in each claim only part of the sentence is said by two passages: the gods in claim 1, reason’s turn toward others in claim 2 (the phrase is the editor’s), the rotten and the old and the person who knows nature in claim 3. The rest of each claim is one passage’s. That what I was made for is reason is the editor’s step; no passage of this section says it.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, taking the universe’s side gains two witnesses, and the article gains what Marcus leaves out here: the hard things, paid willingly as a tax; words for a setback; a test for prayer; how to stand under pain; an answer when a death seems too early; and what holds if I doubt it. He backs nothing in the first claim, and he limits the second: he does not desire hardship itself.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands and takes in the hard things: I take the whole’s side, and what is hard in what it brings I pay willingly, as a tax on being alive. He does not say that hardship itself is to be wished for.

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: this is how I have been formed: I do not obey god but agree with him
piece.follows: Seneca has been formed to agree with God and not to obey him.
piece.context: Seneca answers a complaining Lucilius. To “agree with him” is to agree with God about the illness and losses Seneca has just listed as his own, which he says are decreed and are not accidents.
gives: I take the universe’s side

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: Let whatever has pleased god please man
piece.follows: Whatever has pleased God should please a person as well.
piece.context: On the inner defence against Fortune: not being indignant at what happens to one. What “has pleased god” is whatever happens, including what seems to bring harm.
gives: I take the universe’s side

items.label: action
items.t: The hard things are a tax on being alive, and I pay it willingly. Whatever makes me groan or take fright is part of that tax, and I do not hope to be exempt from it or ask to be.
items.why: In this section Marcus calls what comes fruit and says it is timely; none of his passages names the hard part of it. Seneca names it, and calls it a tax, not a fruit. He says how to receive it: willingly. He does not say that I should want it.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: I shall pay no tax unwillingly.
support.follows: Seneca will pay every tax he owes, and none of them unwillingly.
support.context: From Letter 96, where Seneca tells Lucilius to agree with God. The “tax” is not money: the next sentence says that the taxes of life are everything at which we groan or take fright.
gives: I pay it willingly

support.author: seneca
support.quote: And all the things at which we groan, at which we take fright, are the taxes of life: from these, my Lucilius, do not hope for exemption and do not ask for it.
support.follows: What makes us groan or take fright is one of the taxes of life, and we should neither hope for exemption from it nor ask for it.
support.context: Said to Lucilius, who had feared for his life in an illness. The things that make us groan are the illness, losses, toil and fear listed just before.
gives: The hard things are a tax on being alive
Whatever makes me groan or take fright is part of that tax
I do not hope to be exempt from it or ask to be

items.label: practice
items.t: Whenever something turns out otherwise than I had reckoned, I say: “The gods decided better.”
items.why: Marcus gives words to say of the world: “Dear city of Zeus”. Seneca gives words to say at each setback. They say that what the gods decided is better than what I had reckoned; they do not say, as 10.21 does, that it is good for me.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: say this whenever something has turned out otherwise than you had reckoned: “The gods decided better.”
support.follows: When something turns out otherwise than I had reckoned, I should say that the gods decided better.
support.context: On holding what Fortune gives without leaning on it. He first offers another line for every mishap, then this one, as braver and more just.
gives: Whenever something turns out otherwise than I had reckoned
The gods decided better

items.label: practice
items.t: I speak with God as if other people heard me. The day I ask for nothing that I could not ask for openly, I am released from my desires.
items.why: 5.7 says to pray simply and like a free person, and gives no test. Seneca gives one, and ties it to freedom as well: whoever asks only for what he could ask for openly is released from his desires.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Know that you are released from all desires at the point when you have come to ask god for nothing except what you can ask for openly.
support.follows: A person is released from his desires once he asks God only for what he could ask for openly.
support.context: Seneca has just told Lucilius to drop his old prayers and ask for a sound mind. The saying is Athenodorus’s; to ask “openly” is to ask only for what others may hear.
gives: The day I ask for nothing that I could not ask for openly, I am released from my desires

support.author: seneca
support.quote: live with people just as if god saw, speak with god just as if people heard
support.follows: I should live as if God saw me and speak with God as if people heard me.
support.context: Seneca’s own advice, drawn from that saying: people whisper to the gods the shameful prayers they do not want another person to know. To “speak with god” is to pray.
gives: I speak with God as if other people heard me

items.label: breaks
items.t: In pain or illness, if I give way, I am conquered. It is like a wall falling toward me: if I stand against it and push back, it is driven back.
items.why: 8.54 is about an obstacle in my way: I do not force it and I do not fall. Seneca speaks of something else, pain and illness that press on me, and says to stand up to them. He resists suffering that has to be borne; he does not attack an obstacle, so the two do not conflict.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: he will be conquered if he gives way, he will conquer if he braces himself against his pain.
support.follows: Whoever gives way to his pain is conquered; whoever braces himself against it conquers.
support.context: A letter on bearing illness and pain, to Lucilius, who is ill; Seneca recalls his own sickness. The “he” is anyone set in the midst of difficulties, bracing himself against his pain.
gives: if I give way, I am conquered

support.author: seneca
support.quote: if you stand against it and choose to push back, it will be driven back.
support.follows: What bears down on me is driven back if I stand against it and push back.

items.label: breaks
items.role: When a death seems too early
items.t: When a death seems to come too early, I ask which is fairer: that I obey nature, or that nature obey me. How soon I leave a place I must leave anyway does not matter, and a short life can be a complete one.
items.why: The time is this article’s own point: nothing is too early or too late for me. Seneca meets it in one case only, a death that seems to come too soon, and his answer is not Marcus’s. He does not say the time was right; he says the length of a life does not decide whether it is complete.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Which, I beg you, do you judge the fairer: that you should obey nature, or that nature should obey you? And what does it matter how soon you leave a place that must be left in any case?
support.follows: Seneca asks which is fairer, that I obey nature or that nature obey me, and what it matters how soon I leave a place that must be left in any case.
support.context: Lucilius mourned the philosopher Metronax as dead too soon; Seneca calls such complaints railing at Fate. The “place that must be left in any case” is life.
gives: which is fairer: that I obey nature, or that nature obey me
How soon I leave a place I must leave anyway does not matter

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Just as a person can be complete in a smaller build of body, so too a life can be complete in a smaller measure of time.
support.follows: A short life can be a complete life, as a small person can be a complete person.
support.context: Letter 93, on the philosopher Metronax, mourned as dead too soon: a life is to be measured by what was done in it, not by how long it lasted. A life “in a smaller measure of time” is a short life.
gives: a short life can be a complete one

items.label: doubt
items.role: Even if it is a disaster
items.t: Even if what comes is a disaster, a loss or a wrong, it has no more power against my virtue than a mist has against the sun: my virtue shines less, but it is not smaller.
items.why: No passage of Marcus in this section asks what holds if what comes is not good for me. Seneca’s answer is that even a disaster cannot make virtue smaller. He uses the sun for it, as 8.54 uses a sunbeam for the mind.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: the things set in the way of virtue take nothing away from it: it is not smaller, but it shines less.
support.follows: The things set in virtue’s way take nothing away from it; it only shines less.
support.context: Seneca argues that a good man is happy even under misfortune. What is “set in the way of virtue” stands there as an object stands before the sun, which is no smaller for it.
gives: my virtue shines less, but it is not smaller

support.author: seneca
support.quote: And so disasters and losses and wrongs have the same power against virtue that a mist has against the sun.
support.follows: Disasters, losses and wrongs have no more power against virtue than a mist has against the sun.
support.context: The conclusion of that comparison: a mist hides the sun and takes nothing from it. The “virtue” is the good man’s, which Seneca holds to be his whole good.
gives: Even if what comes is a disaster, a loss or a wrong
it has no more power against my virtue than a mist has against the sun

items.t: Seneca stops short of Marcus’s word “love”. He agrees with God and receives what befalls him without complaint (Ep. 96.2), but he says he is not so mad as to desire a hardship: what he wants is the virtue that bears it. This limits the claim and does not contradict it. He would rather be spared beforehand and agrees once it comes; and of his own death he says he should want whatever the situation demands (Ep. 61.3).

support.author: seneca
support.quote: I am not so mad as to desire to be ill; but if I have to be ill, I shall wish to do nothing without self-control, nothing womanish.
support.follows: Seneca does not want illness; if he has to be ill, what he wants is to do nothing without self-control and nothing weak in it.
support.context: Lucilius asked whether every good is to be wished for, since bravery under torture is a good. Seneca separates the hardship, which he does not want, from his conduct in it.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: So it is not the hardships that are to be wished for, but the virtue by which the hardships are borne.
support.follows: What is to be wished for is not hardship but the virtue by which hardship is borne.
support.context: Seneca’s own summing-up of his answer to that question. The “hardships” are the torture, war and illness he has just named.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: So let us set our mind in order so that we want whatever the situation demands
support.follows: I should bring my mind to want whatever the situation demands.
support.context: Seneca, now old, writes that dying well means dying gladly and that one should do nothing unwillingly. What the situation demands is, above all, his death.

passages.title: On accepting hardship without complaint
passages.text: These things are decreed; they are not accidents. If you trust me at all, I am at this very moment uncovering my inmost feelings to you: in all the things that seem adverse and hard, this is how I have been formed: I do not obey god but agree with him; I follow him from the heart, not because it is necessary. Nothing will ever befall me that I shall receive gloomily, that I shall receive with a sour face; I shall pay no tax unwillingly. And all the things at which we groan, at which we take fright, are the taxes of life: from these, my Lucilius, do not hope for exemption and do not ask for it.

passages.title: On virtue as the only safe good
passages.text: Let him not be indignant at anything that happens to him, and let him know that the very things by which he seems to be harmed serve to preserve the universe and are among those that bring the course of the world and its task to completion. Let whatever has pleased god please man. For this very reason let him admire himself and what is his: that he cannot be conquered, that he holds evils themselves beneath him, that by reason, and nothing is stronger than reason, he subdues chance and pain and wrong.

passages.title: On not depending on fortune's gifts
passages.text: Or rather, by Hercules, so that I may reach for a line that is braver and more just, one with which you may prop up your mind more, say this whenever something has turned out otherwise than you had reckoned: “The gods decided better.” Nothing will happen to one so settled. And he will be so settled if he has reckoned, before he has felt it, with what the changeableness of human affairs can do, if he has children and wife and property as one who will not necessarily have them always, and as one who will not be more wretched on that account if he stops having them.

passages.title: On being alone with yourself
passages.text: But, to send this letter with some small gift as is my habit, what I found in Athenodorus is true: “Know that you are released from all desires at the point when you have come to ask god for nothing except what you can ask for openly.” For as things are, how great is the madness of people! They whisper the most shameful prayers to the gods; if anyone brings his ear close, they will fall silent, and what they do not want a human being to know they tell to god. See, then, whether this might not be a wholesome precept to give: live with people just as if god saw, speak with god just as if people heard. Farewell.

passages.title: On bearing illness and pain
passages.text: Set in the very midst of difficulties, let him say, “Perhaps one day it will be pleasant to remember even these things.” Let him fight back with his whole mind; he will be conquered if he gives way, he will conquer if he braces himself against his pain. As things are, what most people do is this: they pull down on themselves the collapse they ought to be standing against. That thing which presses, which hangs overhead, which bears down: if you begin to draw yourself out from under it, it will follow and weigh more heavily; if you stand against it and choose to push back, it will be driven back.

passages.title: On the quality not length of life
passages.text: Which, I beg you, do you judge the fairer: that you should obey nature, or that nature should obey you? And what does it matter how soon you leave a place that must be left in any case? What we must take care of is not that we live long but that we live enough; for to live long you need fate, to live enough you need the mind. A life is long if it is full; and it is made full when the mind has given back to itself its own good and has transferred to itself the power over itself.

passages.title: On the quality not length of life
passages.text: Just as a person can be complete in a smaller build of body, so too a life can be complete in a smaller measure of time. Years are among the external things. How long I am to be is not mine: to be, for as long as I will be, is mine. Demand this of me: that I do not travel the whole length of an obscure lifetime as if through darkness, that I lead my life, not that I am carried past it.

passages.title: On reason and virtue sufficing for happiness
passages.text: In the same way, the things set in the way of virtue take nothing away from it: it is not smaller, but it shines less. To us, perhaps, it does not show and gleam as much; to itself it is the same, and like the sun when it is obscured it exerts its force out of sight. And so disasters and losses and wrongs have the same power against virtue that a mist has against the sun.

passages.title: On whether enduring hardship is desirable
passages.text: Draw distinctions among these things, my Lucilius, and you will understand that there is something in them to be wished for. I would want torture to be far from me; but if it has to be endured, I shall wish to carry myself in it bravely, honourably, with spirit. Why would I not prefer that war not break out? But if it does break out, I shall wish to bear wounds, to bear hunger and everything that the necessity of war brings, nobly. I am not so mad as to desire to be ill; but if I have to be ill, I shall wish to do nothing without self-control, nothing womanish. So it is not the hardships that are to be wished for, but the virtue by which the hardships are borne.

passages.title: On being ready and willing to die
passages.text: Take care that you never do anything unwillingly. Whatever is going to be necessary for one who resists is no necessity for one who wants it. This is what I mean: the man who takes orders willingly escapes the bitterest part of slavery: doing what he does not want to do. It is not the man who does something under orders who is wretched, but the man who does it unwillingly. So let us set our mind in order so that we want whatever the situation demands, and above all so that we think of our own end without sadness.

claims.role: What comes is good, and on time
claims.t: What the whole brings me is good for me, and it comes at the right time: nothing that is timely for the whole is too early or too late for me.

claims.changed: 10.21 says “each”; the claim says “me”, as 4.19 does. 4.19 speaks to the universe and to nature as “you”; the claim speaks about them and calls both “the whole”, 10.21’s word.

single.quote: Surely the sun does not think it should do the rain’s part? Or Asclepius the part of the fruit-bearing goddess? And what of each of the stars? Are they not different, yet working together toward the same thing?
single.label: Different parts, one work
single.t: The sun does not do the rain’s part, and no god does another’s. The parts of the world differ, and they work together toward the same thing.
single.why: Only this passage speaks of the parts of the world and their separate tasks. No second passage of the section says it, so it is not fused.
single.follows: Each power keeps to its own part; the parts differ and work together toward the same thing.

single.quote: All things from you, all things in you, all things into you.
single.label: One source
single.t: Everything is from nature, in nature, and goes into nature.
single.why: Only this passage says it. It names a source, a place and a destination; it does not say that things work toward an end.
single.follows: All things are from nature, in nature and go into nature.

single.quote: One man says, “Dear city of Cecrops.” But you, will you not say, “Dear city of Zeus”?
single.label: A practice
single.t: As one man says “Dear city of Cecrops” of Athens, I say “Dear city of Zeus”.
single.why: Only this passage gives words to say. They are kept as the article’s practice.
single.follows: If one man can call Athens dear, I am asked to say “Dear city of Zeus”.

single.quote: A prayer of the Athenians: “Rain, rain, dear Zeus, down on the ploughland of the Athenians and the plains.” Either one should not pray, or one should pray like this: simply and like a free person.
single.label: A practice · how to pray
single.t: If I pray, I pray simply and like a free person, as the Athenians prayed for rain on their land.
single.why: Only this passage speaks of prayer. It says how to pray, not for whom.
single.follows: If one prays at all, one should pray as in this prayer: simply and like a free person.

single.quote: It should not lean on the obstacles it meets with force or like a torrent, nor fall down, but stand and light up whatever receives it. For whatever does not give the beam passage will deprive itself of the beam.
single.label: Meeting an obstacle
single.t: When something stands in my way, I do not force my way and I do not fall. I stand and give light to whatever receives it; what gives the light no passage deprives itself of it.
single.why: Only this passage says how to meet what resists me. It shows what failing looks like, forcing or falling, and the way back.
single.follows: Meeting an obstacle, thought should neither force its way nor fall, but stand and light up what receives it.

members.text:
The earth, saith the poet, doth often long after the rain. So is
the glorious sky often as desirous to fall upon the earth, which argues
a mutual kind of love between them. And so (say I) doth the world bear
a certain affection of love to whatsoever shall come to pass With thine
affections shall mine concur, O world. The same (and no other) shall the
object of my longing be which is of thine. Now that the world doth love
it is true indeed so is it as commonly said, and acknowledged ledged,
when, according to the Greek phrase, imitated by the Latins, of things
that used to be, we say commonly, that they love to be.
members.english: “The earth loves the rain, and the holy sky loves,” and the universe loves to bring about whatever is to come. So I say to the universe: “I love along with you.” And is that, too, perhaps said in this sense: “this loves to happen”?

members.text:
The sun seemeth to be shed abroad. And indeed it is diffused but
not effused. For that diffusion of it is a τάσις or an extension. For
therefore are the beams of it called ἀκτῖνες from the word ἐκτείνεσθαι
to be stretched out and extended. Now what a sunbeam is, thou mayest
know if thou observe the light of the sun, when through some narrow
hole it pierceth into some room that is dark. For it is always in a
direct line. And as by any solid body, that it meets with in the way
that is not penetrable by air, it is divided and abrupted, and yet
neither slides off, or falls down, but stayeth there nevertheless: such
must the diffusion in the mind be; not an effusion, but an extension.
What obstacles and impediments soever she meeteth within her way, she
must not violently, and by way of an impetuous onset light upon them;
neither must she fall down; but she must stand, and give light unto
that which doth admit of it. For as for that which doth not, it is its
own fault and loss, if it bereave itself of her light.
members.english: The sun seems to be poured down, and indeed it is poured in every direction, yet it is not poured out. For this pouring is an extension; its beams, at any rate, are called aktines (“rays”) from ekteinesthai (“to be extended”). You could see what a ray is if you watched the sun’s light coming through something narrow into a shaded room. For it extends in a straight line and leans, so to speak, against whatever solid thing it meets that shuts off the air beyond; there it stands, and it does not slip down or fall. So the pouring and spreading of thought should be like that: in no way a pouring out, but an extension. It should not lean on the obstacles it meets with force or like a torrent, nor fall down, but stand and light up whatever receives it. For whatever does not give the beam passage will deprive itself of the beam.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek instead of Casaubon. Passage numbers stay Casaubon’s. In modern editions 10.21 is 10.20, 10.22 is 10.21, 4.19 is 4.23, 6.38 is 6.43 and 8.54 is 8.57; 5.7 is the same.
Reads “the nature of the whole” (10.21), the universe and nature addressed in 4.19, and the universe of 10.22 as one whole.

Keeps only two fused claims. In claim 1 both passages say that what nature brings is good for the one it is brought to, and both speak of its time. In claim 2 the words the two share, “I take the universe’s side”, are the editor’s summary of two sentences spoken to the universe. The parts of the world working together (6.38) and all things from, in and into nature (4.19) are each said by one passage and stand alone.
Withdraws the earlier claim that I pray “for everyone, not for myself alone”. It rested on a clause Casaubon added to 5.7; the Greek ends at “simply and like a free person”.
Reads “Dear city of Zeus” (4.19) as said of the world. The Greek does not say what the city of Zeus is.
Leaves out the poet’s line and the last sentence of 10.22, a remark on a Greek turn of phrase.
articles.limit: Article 3 already says that I accept whatever happens. What this article adds is the time: what comes is good when it comes, never too early or too late. It adds little else. Six passages give two fused claims, and 4.19 feeds both, so the article leans on one passage. It states a trust and does not argue for it.
